entries.title: Luke 1:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: OR, have attempted, but not effected. Hence some ([ilegible].) have concluded, that Luke wrote [ilegible] of the four Evangelists. Howbeit the common opinion is (and the most ancient copies say as much) that Matthew wrote his Gospel eight yeers [ilegible] Christ, Marke ten, Luke fifteen, and John forty two.

entries.title: Luke 1:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Therefore it may seem his Gospel was not dictated to him by Paul (who was no eye-witnesse) as some Ancients have affirmed. But if we can beleeve Tacitus or [ilegible] in things that fell out long before they were born, because we are confident of their diligence in enquiring: how much more should we beleeve Saint Luke upon such doubted assurance, &c?

entries.title: Luke 1:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Or, Following ([ilegible],) them close at heels, (and as we say) hot-foot.

From the very first] Or, from above, as inspired from heaven. ([ilegible].)

To write [ilegible] in order] Distinctly, and yet [ilegible], A ([ilegible].) singular praise in an Historian, for the which, Ambrose much [ilegible] our [ilegible] above [ilegible] the other.

entries.title: Luke 1:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Which thou hast ([ilegible].) received by hear-say, or by word of mouth: and wherein thou hast been catechised, receiving the mysteries of the faith by the ministry of the voyce. And surely when we see men caring and [ilegible] how to finde out this certainty here spoken of, and not to [ilegible] led by conjecturall suppositions, but be fully perswaded as St. Luke was, and would have his Theophilus to be, then there will be some hopes that the Lords parts will increase.

entries.title: Luke 1:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Herod a stranger, upon the death of Antigonus, last of the Maccabeans, by Augustus his favour, was made King of Judaea, and reigned 34. yeers. After [ilegible] and his sonnes death, Judaea was again reduced into a Roman Province; and the government thereof committed unto Pontius Pilate, then to Petronius, after him to Foelix, Festus, Albinus and Florus, whose cruelty provoked the Jewes to rebellion and warre, to their utter overthrow.

Of the course of Abia] According to their weekly waitings at the Altar: 1 Chron. 24. God would not have his Ministers overwrought, though he require them to labour according to their strength, even unto lassitude. But how thanklesse is their labour, that do wilfully over-spend themselves!

entries.title: Luke 1:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
That is, in all the duties of both the Morall and Ceremoniall Law.

Blamelesse] Sine [ilegible], saith the Vulgar, without complaint. ([ilegible].) They neither complained of others, nor were complained of by (Camp. Elisab. fol. 495.) others. As it is reported of Burleigh, Lord Treasurer in Queen Elizabeths reign, that he never sued any man, nor did any man ever sue him: and was therefore in the number of those few, that both lived and died with glory.

entries.title: Luke 1:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Which was then held an heavie judgement, as that which rendred them suspected of impiety: sith Godlinesse had the promise of increase both within doores and without.

entries.title: Luke 1:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He took but his turn, and served but his time. God never purposed to burthen any of his creatures with devotion.

entries.title: Luke 1:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In the incense of prayer, how many sweet spices are burned together, by the fire of Faith, as humility, love, &c?

entries.title: Luke 1:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Cant. 3. 6. the Church is said to ascend out of the wildernesse of this world with pillars of smoak, elationibus fumi, that is with affections, thoughts, desires toward heaven. And although she be black as smoak, in regard of infirmities, yet hath she a principle to [ilegible] her upwards.

entries.title: Luke 1:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As Satan (Zach. 3. 1.) stood at the right hand of Jehoshuah to molest him: So stand the Angels at our right hand, in the publick Assemblies especially to withstand him. And to signifie this, the curtains of the Tabernacle were wrought full of Cherubins within and without.

entries.title: Luke 1:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But without cause: he should have been comforted rather; for his sins were covered. How will wicked men stand before Christ?

entries.title: Luke 1:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Both for a Son, and for a Saviour.

entries.title: Luke 1:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This is not every fathers happinesse. Many fathers are forced through greif for their untoward children to wish to die, as Elias did when he sat under the juniper: and as Moses did when wearied out by the people, Numb. 11. 15.

entries.title: Luke 1:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Significatur singularis [ilegible] praestantia, ut Gen. 10. 9. He shalbe singularly qualified.

entries.title: Luke 1:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An high honour to have any hand in the conversion of souls. They that wise others shall shine in heaven, Dan. 12. 2.

entries.title: Luke 1:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
There is a great agreement between the times of Elias and John Baptist. Herod answereth to Ahab, Herodias to Jezabel, &c.

The disobedient to the wisdom of the just] i. e. By his preaching he shall turn the hearts of the Gentiles to the Jewes, and by his ([ilegible]. Antiq. lib. 18. c. 7.) Baptisme tye them up, as it were, togerher. He made them (according to the phrase that Josephus useth of him) to convent or knit together in Baptisme.

entries.title: Luke 1:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thus Reason will be encroaching upon the bounds of Faith, till she be taken captive by infidelity. Drive therefore Hagar out of doors.

entries.title: Luke 1:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ut apparitor, ab apparendo, ready prest to any service.

entries.title: Luke 1:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: His tongue that so lately moved through unbelief is now tyed up. God will not passe by the well-meant weaknesses of his own, without a sensible check. He was also deaf as well as dumb: hence they made signs to him, vers. 62.

entries.title: Luke 1:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They would not away without the blessing, prescribed to the Preists, Numb. 6. In the Councell of Agathon it was decreed, that people should not presume to go out of the Temples, before the Ministers had blessed ([ilegible]. [ilegible].) the Congregation.

entries.title: Luke 1:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hereupon a Divine thus descants: Tacuit pater vocis, & cessit in miraculum: Vox [ilegible], cedit in contradictionem. Nunquid aeque obmutescit [ilegible] & filius? Johannes & Zacharias? Nunquid & praeco [ilegible] ost? Let us lean to the Papists (saith another) Ministrorum muta officia, populi caeca obsequia, their Ministers, dumb Offices; their peoples, blind obedience.

entries.title: Luke 1:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Zachary, though he ceased to speak, yet he ceased not to minister. Though he were dumb, yet he was not lame, but could do sacrifices, and did it. We may not straight take occasions of with-drawing our selves from the publick services.

entries.title: Luke 1:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Obscurum qua id fecerit ex causa. Its hard to say wherefore she did this, saith a learned Interpreter: but, likely, out of modesty; and that she may make no shew, till she were sure; as also that the miracle might appear the greater.

entries.title: Luke 1:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: She saw that all her prayers, that she had haply forgot, were not lost, but laid up with God, who now sends in the blessing, that she had despaired of. The Lord oft doth things for his people that they look not for, Isaith 64. and stayes so long, that when he comes, he finds not Faith, Luke 18. 8.

entries.title: Luke 1:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: God and his Angels can find out his hidden ones, Psal. 83. 3. in what corner of the country soever.

entries.title: Luke 1:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: 1 The better to free her from suspition of fornication. 2 That she might have one to provide for her, when she was with Child. 3 That the mystery of (Sensim sine sensu.) God manifested in the flesh might come to light by little and little.

entries.title: Luke 1:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A salutation, ([ilegible].) and not a prayer as Papists pervert and abuse it. And when the Ave-Mary-Bell rings, which is at Sun-rising, Noon, and Sunsetting, all men in what place soever, house, field, street, or market do presently kneel down, and send up their united devotions (Sands his Survey.) to heaven by an Ave-Maria. Also, where one fasteth on Friday, which they count our Lords day, many fast on Saturday, which they count our Ladies day.

entries.title: Luke 1:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Affect not the vain praises of men, saith one. The blessed Virgin was troubled, when truly praised of an Angel. They shall be praised of Angels in heaven, who have eschewed the praises of men on earth.

What manner of salutation] Cujus esset (saith one Interpreter) voluit enim probare spiritum. Qualis & quanta, saith another: Id est, quam honorifica & magnifica, ac proinde supra sortem suam pofita. What an honourable salutation it was, and more then she could acknowledge.

entries.title: Luke 1:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: We are not fit to hear, till quit of carnall affections and passions. The eare which tastes words, as the mouth doth meat, when filled with choller or other ill humours, can relish no comfort.

entries.title: Luke 1:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matt. 1. 21. If it were such a mercy to Israel that God raised up of their Sonnes for Prophets, and of their young men for Nazarites, Amos 2. 11. What was it to Mary and in her to all mankind, that she should be mother to the Arch-prophet, to that famous Nazarite?

entries.title: Luke 1:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Answerable to the Hebrew Elion, whence [ilegible] for the sunne, cujus antiquissima veneratio, saith Beza, whom the ancients deifie.

entries.title: Luke 1:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: St. Paul saith indeed that he shall at the end of the world deliver up the Kingdome to God the Father: not that his Kingdom shall then cease, but that form of administration only, that he now useth in the collecting and conserving of his Church.

entries.title: Luke 1:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This is a speech not of unbeleif, but of wonderment, as desiring also to be better informed.

entries.title: Luke 1:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As once he did the confused Chaos in the Creation: This very, expression was a great confirmation to the Virgins faith, and may well serve for a caution to us not to be over-curious in searching into this secret.

entries.title: Luke 1:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It is observed that the barren women (so called in both Testaments) had the best Children, as Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Elizabeth, &c. because long held off, and much humbled. Some also have observed that the (D. Hall's Contemplat. on the New Test.) New Testament affords more store of good women then the Old.

entries.title: Luke 1:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: We never doubt of Gods will, but we do in some measure doubt of his power. See them both running paralell, Job 42. 2.

entries.title: Luke 1:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not Mall Gods (Staffords Female Glory.) maid, as a black-mouthed Blatero hath blasphemed in print, that the Puritans rudely call her.

entries.title: Luke 1:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of Juda, southward of Jerusalem, into the City of Hebron, Josh. 21. 9.

entries.title: Luke 1:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To whom she could not rest till she had imparted the good newes, and both given and received some spirituall gift for mutuall confirmation and comfort, Rom. 1. 11, 12 Greif growes greater by concealing, joy by expression. Only the meeting of Saints in heaven can parallell the meeting of these two couzens.

entries.title: Luke 1:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Such comfort there is in the presence of Christ (though but in the womb) as it made John to spring. What then shall it be in heaven, think we?

entries.title: Luke 1:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
So is Jael the wife of Heber said to be, Judg. 5. 24. who yet perhaps was hardly so good a woman as Deborah, that called her so. But it was no small confirmation to the blessed Virgin, to hear the same words from Elizabeth, that she heard before from the Angell.

And blessed is the fruit, &c.] Or, because blessed is the fruit of thy womb, therefore blessed art thou, &c.

entries.title: Luke 1:43
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That the Lord himself should come amongst us, as he did in the flesh, and doth still by his Spirit, Oh what a mercy!

entries.title: Luke 1:44
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: More like a suckling at the ([ilegible] [ilegible], 1 Pet. 2. 2.) the breast (as the word signifieth) then an Embryo in the womb. The Spirit then worketh, even in unborn babes that are elect, some kind of saving knowledge of Christ, answerable to faith in those that are grown up.

entries.title: Luke 1:45
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Mary beleeved: so did not [ilegible], though a man, a Priest, aged, learned, eminent, and the message to him of more appearing possibility. This, Elizabeth here seems to have an eye to.

Beleeved that there shall be, &c.] The same may be said of every beleiver. It is true also in cases ordinary: A perswasion that God will help and keep us will indeed help and keep us, Marke 9. 23.

entries.title: Luke 1:46
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
See the benefit of good [ilegible], and how one Christian kindleth another. As Iron sharpneth iron, so [ilegible] the face of a man his freind. (Prov. 27.)

Doth magnifie the Lord] Makes roome for him, enlargeth her ([ilegible].) thoughts of him, throwes wide open the everlasting doors, that the King of glory may come in, in State.

My spirit rejoyceth] Tripudiat, danceth a galliard (which ([ilegible].) seemeth to come from the Greek word here used) danceth ([ilegible]. Super Deo.) Levaltoes in God, or for God my Saviour, as the matter and ground of my joy.

entries.title: Luke 1:48
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Vilitatem, the [ilegible] and abject [ilegible]. (See [ilegible]. in loc.) Cóntra Mariae [ilegible], quae [ilegible] Papicolae. Here's no mention of merit.

All generations shall call me blessed] How much more should we with one mind and one mouth blesse. God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ? This is an honour that he much standeth upon, Rom. 15. 6.

entries.title: Luke 1:49
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
[ilegible] The mighty strong ([ilegible]) God.

Hath done great things for me] No small things can fall from so great a hand. He gives life himself.

And Holy is his [ilegible]] God that is holy is to be sanctified in holinesse, Isaiah 5. 16. when men see their children especially (as here) the work of Gods hands, Isaiah 29. 23.

entries.title: Luke 1:50
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Personall goodnesse is profitable to posterity.

entries.title: Luke 1:51
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
It appears by the whole frame of this holy song, that the blessed Virgin was well versed iu the Scripture, which she here makes so much use of in sundry passages. She was eruditionis pietatis & modestiae [ilegible], as one speaketh of the Lady Jane Gray.

He hath scattered the proud] He by his strong Arme hath ([ilegible].) so splitted them, that they shiver into peeces: or hath made them as darts, which being among the enemies, are lost: or hath hurled them hither and thither, as the wind doth the dust of the mountains.

entries.title: Luke 1:52
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As he did [ilegible] the proud Turk, and set up Tamberlaine a Stythian shepheard; who said that he was sent from heaven to punish Bajazets rashnesse; (Turk. Hist.) and to teach him that the proud are hated of God, whose promise is to pluck down the mighty, and raise up the lowly.

entries.title: Luke 1:53
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See [ilegible] Note on Matth. 5. 6.

entries.title: Luke 1:54
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He hath put under his ([ilegible]) hand, and raised him prostrate, taken him up at his feet. This he will not do for an evill doer: he taketh not the ungodly by the hand, Job 8. 20.

entries.title: Luke 1:55
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who lived upon reversions, and dyed upon the promises, accounting them good free-hold. God keeps promise with nights and dayes, [ilegible] 33. 20. 25. How much more will he, with Abraham, and his seed for ever?

entries.title: Luke 1:56
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An honest heart is where its calling is. Such a one, when [ilegible] is abroad, is like a fish in the aire; whereinto if it leap for recreation or necessity, yet it soon returns to its own element.

entries.title: Luke 1:57
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The voice of the Lord maketh the Hindes to calve, Psal. 29. 9. though of all other bruit creatures they bring forth with great trouble, bowing themselves, bruising their [ilegible], and casting out their sorrows, Job 39. 4. 6. How much [ilegible] will [ilegible] help his dear handmaids?

entries.title: Luke 1:58
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the greater, [ilegible] in her old age. Births, with those that are ancienter, are with greater danger: so is the new birth in old sinners.

entries.title: Luke 1:59
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Infants are no innocents, they are conceived in sin, and the first sheet or blanket wherewith they are covered is woven of sin, shame, bloud and filth, Ezek. 16. 4. 6. They were Circumcised, to signifie that we had bettet be stayed, and have our skin quite stript off, then to haue it as a skinbottle hanging in the smoak of filthy desires, and blown full of [ilegible] motions with the breath of Satan.

entries.title: Luke 1:60
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bucer here observeth that he that was high Preist when Salomon built the Temple, was called (Bucer. in [ilegible].) John: and that there was herein a sweet suitablenesse. [ilegible] vero connenit, saith he, ut quo nomine sacerdos Salomonis typici, hoc & veri vocaretur: that the Type and Truth might accord in the very name.

entries.title: Luke 1:61
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: There is an inbred desire in us all of immortality: we would eternize our names, and do therefore call our children, cities, lands, &c. after them, Psal. 49. 11. But they do best that get assurance that their names are written in heaven. They that depart from God shall be written in the earth, Jeremiah 17. 13. as Cains son, Lord Enoch of Enoch, Genesis 4. And those men of renown, Genesis 11. 4 were.

entries.title: Luke 1:62
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who therefore seems to have been deaf (as well as dumb) because he had not hearkned to the Angels speech, but gain-saied it.

entries.title: Luke 1:63
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Tabellam sc. [ilegible], in qua olim stylo [ilegible], saith Sa. He had an excellent faculty of whom Martiall reporteth, (Martial. lib. [ilegible] de Notario.) Currant verba licet, manus est veocior illis: Et vix lingua suum, dextra peregit opus.

entries.title: Luke 1:64
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And had he had as many tongues as he had hairs upon his head, he could never have sufficiently praised God for his son, but especially for his Saviour. See 1 Timothy 1. 15, 16, 17. Zachary beleeveth and therefore speaks, Psal. 116. 10. the tongue of the dumb sings, Isaiah 35. 6.

entries.title: Luke 1:65
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This was either the fear of admiration at the many strange accidents about the birth of the Baptist; or the fear of punishment, seeing so good a man as Zachary ([ilegible]. de [ilegible].) so long to have suffered for his unbeleef.

entries.title: Luke 1:66
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, his grace and blessing. He had the honour to be Legis & gratiae fibula, as Chrysologus hath it; the buckle and boundary of the Law and Gospel.

entries.title: Luke 1:67
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This was a plentifull amends for the late losse of his speech. See here the goodnesse of God to all his; Quibus non solum ablata restituit `sed [ilegible] concedit (saith Ambrose) Ille dudum [ilegible] Prophetat. God is better to his then their hopes.

entries.title: Luke 1:68
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This is [ilegible] Evangelicissimus, say both Bucer and Pellican. A most Evangelicall Canticle.

Redeemed his people] From the wrath of God over them; the guilt and power of sin within them; from Satan and the punishment of sin without them.

entries.title: Luke 1:69
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A Cornu-copia, or a mighty Saviour, qui instar bovis cornupetae inimicos populi Dei prosternat atque dejiciat, that can bestir him much better then that Heegoate, (Piscat.) Alexander the great, who had a notable horn between his eyes, wherewith he cast down the Ramme to the ground and stamped upon him, &c. Dan. 8. 7. Macedones tunc temporis AEgeades, id est caprini dicti sunt. Occasionem vide Justin. lib. 7. The Macedones were at that time called Goate-sprung.

entries.title: Luke 1:70
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: There were many Prophets, yet had they all but one mouth: so sweet is their harmony.

entries.title: Luke 1:71
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Salvation from our enemies. This properly importeth the privative part of mans happinesse, but includes the positive too.

entries.title: Luke 1:72
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gods love moves him to promise, his truth binds him to performe. See both these, 2 Sam. 7. 18. 21. For thy words sake, and according to thine owne heart: (that is, ex mero motu) haste thou done all these things.

entries.title: Luke 1:73
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: [ilegible] a hedge, [ilegible] a man may not break: much lesse will God.

entries.title: Luke 1:74
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Servati sumus ut serviamus. Christ hath therefore broke the devils yoke from of our necks, that we may take upon us this sweet yoke, and not carry ourselves as sons of Belial.

entries.title: Luke 1:75
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The sense of Gods presence makes men conscientiously obedient to both tables of the Law. Cave, [ilegible] Cato, was a watch-word among the Romanes. Noli [ilegible], Deus videt, [ilegible] astant, &c. Take heed what thou doest, God beholds thee, Angels observe thee, &c.

entries.title: Luke 1:76
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
scil. qui nunc tantillus es, in virum magnum evades: Though little, thou shalt prove great.

Thou shalt goe before the face of the Lord] Any relation to whom ennobleth, and advanceth all worth.

entries.title: Luke 1:77
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not by infusion, Dan. 1. 17. but by instruction. See the dignity and duty of Ministers.

entries.title: Luke 1:78
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or as Beza rendreth it, ([ilegible].) The Branch from on high, not from beneath, as other plants or branches. So the anchor of hope entreth not into the deep, but into that within the vaile, Heb. 6. 19.

entries.title: Luke 1:79
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This imports 1. continuance, 2. content.

To guide our feet] The superstitious Pagans thought that their (Arnob. advers. Gent. lib. 4.) goddesse Vibilia kept them in their right way when they travelled: But we have a better guide to God.

entries.title: Luke 1:80
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Though his meat was but course, and not so nourishing. The blessing of God is the staffe of bread: bread would no more nourish without it then a piece of earth.

entries.title: Luke 2:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
BY a sweet providence of God, that Christ might be born at Bethlehem, according to the Scriptures. Howbeit Augustus thought not so (as it is said in another case of Nebuchadnezzar, Esay 10.) but ambitiously sought the setting forth of his own greatnesse, and large command, and carried it without punishment; when as David smarted sore for a like offence. But God will take that from others, that he will not bear with in his own. Amos 3. 2.

That all the world] That is, the Romane world: but such was their ambition, that though they had but a part, yet they stiled themselves Lords of all the World. So the Pope (the image of that Beast) will needs be stiled Universall Bishop. The Great Turk (that Eastern Antichrist) calls himselfe God on earth, Sole Monarch of the [ilegible], Commander of all that can be commanded, &c. and by many other such like swelling titles.

entries.title: Luke 2:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Quirinus the Latine Writers call him. Now that the Scepter was departed, Shiloh came.

entries.title: Luke 2:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To pay a certain small sum of money in token of fealty. I was once at a Court-Sermon (saith Melancthon) on the Nativity-day, and this was the Text: but the Preacher, instead of discoursing on Christs [ilegible], (Joh. Manl. loc. [ilegible]. 479.) spent the whole hour, in a very cold day, in perswading the people to obey Magistrates, and to give them as much money as they call for. This is the guise of Court-Parasites, Princes trencher-Flyes.

entries.title: Luke 2:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By a speciall providence of God, as is above-noted, verse 1. and not onely so, but that the holy Virgin might still have with her the keeper and cover of her virginity; that the devill might not have occasion to raise up false reports, about her great belly.

entries.title: Luke 2:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yet could not be excused. This was a cruelty in Augustus (not to spare great-bellied women) but a mercy of God to mankind; for what the [ilegible] had it been for us, if Joseph had gone to Bethlehem, and not Mary also?

entries.title: Luke 2:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Her delivery might well be hastened, or at least facilitated by her long journey; for it was no lesse then foure dayes journey from Nazareth to Bethlehem. Some say she was gravida, but not gravata; great-bellied, but not unweildy: Lumen enim quod in se habebat, pondus [ilegible] non poterat, saith Augustine: but I am not bound to beleeve him.

entries.title: Luke 2:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Whether shee were Deipara, the Mother of God, was a great controversie, and raised a great storm in the Councell of Ephesus; insomuch as the Emperour declared both sides hereticks. But forasmuch as [ilegible] was the Mother of Christ, Mat. 1. 23. and Christ is God, in ([ilegible], [ilegible] [ilegible], ut [ilegible]) bringing forth Christ, she was the Mother of God. Whether she continued after this a Virgin, piè credimus, sed nihil affirmamus. But that shee vowed Virginity, as Papists [ilegible], we deny: For how could she promise Virginity to God, and Marriage to Joseph?

Wrapped him in swadling-[ilegible]] This paines she was at (such ([ilegible] of [ilegible] to rend.) was her love) though newly delivered, and much weakned thereby. His swadling-clothes were poore and ragged, as may be gathered out of the Greek word here used.

Laid him in a manger] Non in aureo reclinatorio, saith Ludolphus, not in a stately room, as the Porphyrogeniti in Constantinople; not in the best but basest place of the Inne, which is counted the meanest house of a City. Oh humble Saviour, whither wilt thou [ilegible]?

entries.title: Luke 2:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
At the tower of [ilegible], say some, between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, where Jacob, returning from Mesopotamia, stayed with his flock, after hee had buried Rachel, Gen. 35. 21. Mic. 4. 8.

By night] Hence some gather, that our Saviour was not born in the winter; because in winter they housed their cattle, and fed them not without doores, Pro. 27. 25.

entries.title: Luke 2:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Gabriel, likely, was sent, not to Zachary or Simeon, &c. but to certain Shepherds. God goes a way by himself. Had the Sages of the East met with these Shepherds, they had received better intelligence then they did from the learned Scribes.

And the glory of the Lord] As when a Kings son is born, [ilegible] are made, &c.

entries.title: Luke 2:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The first Preacher of the Gospel, was an Angel. God hath now taken this honour from the Angels, and put it upon the Ministers, who are in Scripture called Angels, Revel. 2. 1. and Angels Ministers, Heb. 1. 14. The old Church had [ilegible] the promise, we have [ilegible], the [ilegible] tidings.

entries.title: Luke 2:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Greek word is so emphaticall (as ([ilegible]. Cic. in Verr. Act. 4.) Tully witnesseth) that other tongues can hardly find a fit word to expresse it. The Grecians by Flaminius rang out [ilegible] with such a courage, that the birds astonished, fell to the earth.

entries.title: Luke 2:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In vilibus & veteribus indumentis, saith [ilegible]. See the Note on verse 7.

entries.title: Luke 2:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Angels, who have neither so much interest in Christ, nor benefit by him as we, sing him into the world: And shall we be dumb? They sang when the world was created, Job 38. 7. So now that it was repaired by Christ.

entries.title: Luke 2:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Pax, quasi pactio conditionum. [ilegible] [ilegible], à connectendo in unum. Christ is the great Peace-maker; but only to the elect, called here the Men of Gods good will. When he was born, Cuncta atque continua totius (Flor. Hist. l. 4.) generis humani aut pax fuit aut pactio.

entries.title: Luke 2:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They did not reason nor debate with themselves (saith Bishop Hooper Martyr in a Letter to certain good people taken praying in Bow-Churchyard, and now in trouble) who should keep the wolfe from the sheep in the mean time; but committed the sheep to him whose pleasure they obeyed: So let us doe now that we be called; commit all other things to him that called us. He will take heed (Act, and Mon.) that all shall be well. He will help the husband, comfort the wife, guide the servants, keep the house, preserve the goods: yea, rather then it should be undone, he will wash the dishes, rock the cradle, &c.

entries.title: Luke 2:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They, though of the bloud royall, yet lay obscured, not thrusting themselves into observation, but well content with a low condition. Beata Virgo in vili stabulo sedet, & jacet; sed quod homines negligunt, ([ilegible].) coelestes cives honorant & inquirunt, saith Stella. The humble person is like the violet, which growes low, hangs the head downwards, (Bernard.) and hides it selfe with its own leaves. And were it not that the fragrant smell of his many vertues betrayes him to the world, he would chuse to live and dye in his self-contenting [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 2:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: True goodnesse is communicative: there is no envie in spirituall things; because they may be divided in solidum: One may have as much as another, and all alike. These shepherds, as those lepers, 2 King. 7. 9. said one to another, Wee doe not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace, &c.

entries.title: Luke 2:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yet made little benefit of what they heard. All the world wondred after the Beast, Revel. 13. 3. And it was a wonder there was no more wondering at the birth of our Saviour; if that were true especially, that (besides the Wise-mens starre, Mat. 2. and the Angelicall musick in the air, &c.) among the Gentiles a voyce was heard, The great God is now about to be born: And that at Rome, the likenesse of a woman carrying a child in her arms was seen about the sunne, &c. These things are storied. Polydor Virgil reports out of Orosius, (Polyd. Virg. lib. 4. cap. 1.) that on the very day of Christs nativity, Augustus Caesar caused proclamation that no man should stile him Lord any longer, Manifesto praesagio majoris Dominatus, qui tum in terris ortus esset: as presaging a greater then himself then born.

entries.title: Luke 2:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Her soule was as an holy ark: her memory like the pot of Mānnah, preserving holy truthes, and remarkable occurrences.

entries.title: Luke 2:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: God to shew that he respected not persons, revealed this grand mystery to shepheards and Wise-men, the one poor, the other rich; the one learned, the other unlearned; the one Jewes, the other Gentiles; the one neer, the other far off.

entries.title: Luke 2:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ would be Circumcised, and so become bound to fulfill the Law, that hee might free us that were under the Law, Gal. 4. 5.

entries.title: Luke 2:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
She was rather sanctified then polluted by bearing Christ, yet wrangleth not with the Law, nor claimeth an immunity. Now if she were so officious in ceremonies, what in the maine duties of morality?

According to the Law] This Law of Purification proclaimes our uncleannesse, whose very birth infects the mother that bare us. She might not till the seventh day converse with men, nor till the fortieth day appear before God in the Sanctuary, nor then without a burnt-offering for thanksgiving, and a sin-offering for expiation of a double sin, viz. of the Mother that conceived, and of the Son that was conceived.

entries.title: Luke 2:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This proves that Mary brought forth Christ in a naturall way, and not utero clauso, by a miracle, as Papists would have it, to prove their fiction of Transubstantiation.

Shall be called holy to the Lord] God requireth the first-born, as usually best-beloved; that together with our children, he might draw to himself the best of our affections.

entries.title: Luke 2:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christs Mother was not rich enough to bring a Lamb. Let this comfort poor Christians. I know thy poverty, saith Christ, but that's nothing, thou art rich, Revelations 2. 9. Smyrna the poorest Church, hath the highest commendation.

entries.title: Luke 2:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Or wary and cautelous; one that ([ilegible].) takes heed and is fearfull of being deceived in that which he takes for right and currant.

Waiting for the Consolation of Israel] That is for Christs comming: This was the sugar wherewith they sweetned all their crosses: this was the Dittany, by tasting whereof (as Harts do) they shoke of all the peircing shafts of their afflictions. Some Jewes conclude the Messiah when he comes shall be called Menahem the ([ilegible].) comforter, from Lam. 1. 16.

entries.title: Luke 2:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By an immediate Oracle. ([ilegible].) The Idolatrous heathens made use of this word to signifie their impious and diabolicall Oracles. The abuse of a word taketh not away the use of it.

entries.title: Luke 2:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So still, the steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord, Psal. 37. 23. He sets his spirit as a Tutour, to direct and convince [ilegible] into all truth. Simeon likely, had done as Daniel did, Chap. 9. 2. found out by diligent search, that the fulnesse of time was come, and is therefore thus answered from heaven.

entries.title: Luke 2:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The blessed [ilegible] armfull that ever the good old man had in his life. The Patriarchs saluted him, but afar off, Heb. 11. ([ilegible].)

entries.title: Luke 2:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Simeon having (The souls solace.) laid in his heart (saith one) what he lapt in his armes, sung, [ilegible] dimitt as; I fear no sin, I dread no death. I have lived enough, I have my life; I have long'd enough, I have my love; I have seen enough, I have my light: I have served enough, I have my saint: I have sorrowed enough, I have my joy: Sweet babe, let this Psalm serve for a [ilegible] to thee, and for a funerall for me. Oh sleep in my armes, and let me sleep in thy peace. Dying Velcurio broke out into these words, Pater est amator, [ilegible] Redemptor, Spiritus Sanctus Consolator: quomodo itaque tristitiâ affici possim? Dying ([ilegible]. [ilegible]. [ilegible]. [ilegible]. 117.) [ilegible] said, Ego [ilegible] Sanctorum minimus, credo & [ilegible] Christum, salutem [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 2:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A great satisfaction. So it was to Job, Chap. 42. 5. when he could say, I have heard of thee by the hearing of the [ilegible], but now mine eye seeth thee. What shall it be to [ilegible] when we shall see God face to face, &c. 1 Cor. ([ilegible].) 13. 12.? [ilegible] aspe [ilegible]. Worship we God with reverence till we come to see him face to face.

entries.title: Luke 2:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As a banner displaid, as a beacon on a hill, or as the Sun in heaven to be beheld of all: as the brasen serpent was lifted up in the wildernesse, &c. Joh. 3. 15. ([ilegible].) [ilegible]. 2. 11.

entries.title: Luke 2:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Oh! pity their [ilegible], and pray their conversion, that the Jewes may call God Abba, the Gentiles Father, Dan. 12. 11. There is a Prophecy of (Gods waiting to be gracious by Mr. Case. p. 57.) the Jewes finall restauration, (saith one) and the time is expressed which is 1290. years after the ceasing of the daily sacrifice, and the setting up of the abomination of desolation: which is conceived to be about Julians time, who assayed to re-build the Temple of the Jewes, but was hindered from heaven. This was Anno Dom. 360. to which if you adde 1290. yeares, it will pitch the calculation upon the year 1650.

entries.title: Luke 2:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Saints the further they see into the mystery of Christ, the more are they transported with admiration. But most of al at the last day, 2 Thes. 1. 10.

entries.title: Luke 2:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For a but-mark, against whom his enemies shall shoot the shafts of their gain-sayings: Like as at the sack of Constantinople, the Image of the [ilegible] was taken [ilegible] by the Turks, and a Turks cap put upon the head thereof, (Turk. Hist. [ilegible] 347.) and so set up, and shot at with their arrowes, calling it the God of the Christians.

entries.title: Luke 2:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This confutes that of [ilegible]; Mulier nulla cordicitus dolet ex animo. The word (A. Gil. l. 10. c. 25.) here rendred sword properly signifies a long Thracian [ilegible].

That the thoughts of many hearts] As they are also now in these discriminating, shedding times. Affliction tryeth men who are Crocodiles, Spunges, Camelions, &c. Before these dayes came (Act. and Mon. fol. 1482.) (said Master Bradford Martyr) how many thought of themselves, that they had been in Gods bosome, and so were taken, and would be taken in the world? But now we see whose they are: for to whom we obey, his servants we are, &c. In the Palatinate scarce one man in twenty stood out: but fell to Popery, as fast as leaves in autumne.

entries.title: Luke 2:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: i. e. She was a pure virgin when married to her husband. All are not virgins that passe for such: some have their secret conveyances, Prov. 30. 19. 20. They can eate stollen bread, and afterwards so wipe their lips that not the least crum shall be [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 2:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: She was now ripe, and ready, even of her own accord, to fall into Gods hand, as ripe fruites do into the hand of the gatherer. And the thoughts of death had long since forbad the banes of a second marriage. Cogita te qisotidiè mariturum, & de secundis [ilegible] nunquam cogitabis. (Hier. Ep. ad [ilegible].) Think of death, and the thoughts of marrying again will dye within thee.

entries.title: Luke 2:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Succinuit Simeoni, seconded Simeon, and sang the same song. This was somewhat extraordinary, as being against that 1 Tim. 2. 12. and therefore fell out only in troublesome and confused times of the Church; as likewise [ilegible] the Prophetesse. Our Praedicantissae have here no patronage.

entries.title: Luke 2:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This is often recorded of them in this Chapter, that they observe the Law exactly, to their singular commendation. The Law is to be kept as the apple of ones eye, Prov. 7. 2. Count nothing little that God commands. It is as much treason to coyne pence as twenty-shilling-peeces: And they were commanded not to [ilegible] of the bloud, as ever they looked for Gods blessing.

They returned into Galilee] After they had first fled down into AEgypt, Matt. 2.

entries.title: Luke 2:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Without measure; so that of his overflow we have all received grace for grace (John 1. 10.) He had a fulnesse not repletive only, but diffusive too: not of plenty only, but of bounty also, not only of abundance, but of redundancy. Hee was Anointed with the Oyle of gladnesse, not onely above, but for his fellowes.

entries.title: Luke 2:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Every male was to appear thrice a year before the Lord. In the females it was a freewill offering, and well accepted.

entries.title: Luke 2:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: What he did from his infancy hitherto, the Scripture is silent: Papists faine many idle relations, and thereby expose us to the jeares of Jewish and Turkish miscreants. Where the Scripture hath no tongue, we must have no eares.

entries.title: Luke 2:43
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: One would wonder they should be so carelesse of so peerlesse a pearle: They might well think there were enough at Jerusalem, among the [ilegible] especially, that would have been glad to have dispatcht [ilegible] that should take upon them to be Messias the prince, as Daniel calleth him, Chap 9. 25.

entries.title: Luke 2:44
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They knew him to be of a disposition not strange and Stoicall, but sweet and sociable. Let not us tye up our selves in a stern austerity, but run into the company of those now, that must be our everlasting companions in heaven.

entries.title: Luke 2:45
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The best are sometimes at a losse, and hard put too't for three dayes, or so. [ilegible] this, mostly, for their security, as the Church in the [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 2:46
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Christus prius sedet [ilegible] medio Doctorum (ut rectè distin. 36. Gratian.) quam [ilegible] capit munus Mediatoris obire.

Hearing them, and posing them] In this very year the Temple was prophaned, even at the Passeover. For the Priests having [ilegible] the Temple doores by night, as the manner was, found a great company of dead-mens bones in the morning, thrown here and there thorough the whole house. This, saith Josephus, was thought to have been done by the Samaritans in spight to the Jewes. But others think God had a speciall hand in it, to signifie [ilegible] Temple-services were shortly to dye and determine; now ([ilegible]. Chron.) [ilegible] the Lord of heaven and earth had taught therein with his own [ilegible] voice.

entries.title: Luke 2:47
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Which was so large, even as [ilegible], that some have affirmed it to be infinite, and uncreated: [ilegible] of this, his manhood, being a creature, was uncapable. Howbeit here [ilegible] Saviour put forth a beam of his Deity, which yet he soon drew in again, and lay long after obscured.

entries.title: Luke 2:48
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Animo [ilegible], [ilegible] afflictissimo. God often cures a Lethargy of security, by a [ilegible] of perplexity.

entries.title: Luke 2:49
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Men be they pleased or displeased, God must be obeyed.

entries.title: Luke 2:50
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yet were well versed in the [ilegible]. If God give us not sight as well as light, we are still to seek.

entries.title: Luke 2:51
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Labouring with his [ilegible], &c, Mark 6. 5.

entries.title: Luke 2:52
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Being [ilegible] as Macarius was called, whilest a child, for his extraordinary grace and (Niceph.) gravity.

entries.title: Luke 3:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: TAcitus calleth him Procurator only of Judea. But Saint Luke ([ilegible]) here makes little difference betwixt his office and the Imperiall honour of his Master Tiberius: for he useth the same word to expresse both. The Earle of Flanders counts it a great prerogative, that he writes himself Comes Dei gratiâ. Others only Dei clementiâ. The Duke of Millain, that he is the prime Duke of Europe. The Deputy of Ireland, that there commeth no Vicegerent in Europe more neer the Majesty and prerogative of a King then he, &c.

entries.title: Luke 3:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By turnes, Joh. 11. 44. Act. 4. 6. contrary to the old order. Throughout the whole Turkish Territories, there is but one Mufta or HighPriest, and he is the supream Judge and rectifier of all actions, as well Civil as Ecclesiastical.

entries.title: Luke 3:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Johns note was still, Repentance. Christ comes not, where this Herald hath not been before him. Yet now it is come to that passe, that many men scorn to hear a Sermon of Repentance. Its a sign, say some; that the Minister hath been idle that week, or that his stock is spent when he comes to preach of such a common theame as Repentance. If God be not mercifull, we shall quickly dispute away all our Repentance, as a famous preacher justly complaineth.

entries.title: Luke 3:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Called a great ([ilegible] Barathrum.) roule, Esay 8. 1. (because it treates of great things, Maxima in minimo) and said to be written with the Pen of a man, that is cleerly that the simplest of men may understand it, Deuteronomie 30. 11.

entries.title: Luke 3:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Every hole, or hollow. Fainting of heart unfits the way for Christ, as well as the swelling hills of pride. Plain things will joyn in every point one with another; not so, rough and hollow things: so plain spirits close with Gods Truths; not so those that are swolne, and uneven.

entries.title: Luke 3:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Viz. All that order their conversation aright, Psal. 50. 23. which is the life of thankfulnesse. ib.

entries.title: Luke 3:7-9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matthew 3. 7, 8, 9, 10.

entries.title: Luke 3:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. What are those fruits worthy of Repentance, that we in our places must bring forth?

entries.title: Luke 3:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thus Tyrus evidenced her repentance, Isa. 23. 18. by feeding and cloathing Gods Saints with her merchandize. Thus Zacheus, Dorcas, &c. This is all the lesson that for the present he sets them, being but young scholars in the schoole of Christ.

entries.title: Luke 3:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Make no more of your places, then ([ilegible]) ye may with a good conscience. Shun that mystery of iniquity that is crept into most callings. A great part of the Turks Civil Justice (Sands his Travels.) at this day is grounded upon Christs words, Thou shalt not do what thou wouldst not have done to thee.

entries.title: Luke 3:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Shake no man by the shoulders, ([ilegible]) tosse no man to and fro, to put him into a fright, smite no man with the fist of wickednesse. Tamerlaine took such order with his Souldiers that none were injuried by them: If any souldier of his had but taken an apple or the like from any man, he died for it. One of his souldiers having taken a little milk from a country woman, and she thereof complaining, he caused the said souldier to be presently killed, and his stomack to be ript, where the milk (Turk. hist f. 213) that he had of late drunk being found, he contented the woman and so sent her away: who had otherwise undoubtedly dyed for her false accusation, had it not so appeared.

Neither accuse any falsely] Get nothing by sycophancie. Oppresse ([ilegible]) no man either by force or fraud, and forged cavilation, as it is rendred, Luke 19. 8.

entries.title: Luke 3:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yet John did no miracle, but he was a burning and a shining light, he thundered in his doctrine, and lightened in his life. Hence was he so much admired.

entries.title: Luke 3:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By this expression the Baptist acknowledgeth Christs Godhead, as did also Mary by washing his feet. But what doth the Pope that holds forth his feet to be kissed? Is not this he that sits as God in the Temple of God? Is not this Dominus Deus noster Papa? Learned he not this abominable insolency of Dioclesian that bloudy Persecutor? who as he was the first Roman Emperour that would be worshipped (Eatrop.) as God, so he was the first that wore shooes embellished with precious stones, and held forth his feet to be kissed of his prostrate suitors.

entries.title: Luke 3:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Viz. The preaching of the Gospel.

entries.title: Luke 3:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Whom it was not lawfull for Herod to have, though Philip were dead, as Josephus saith he was. This was the case so much controverted (Joseph. Antiq. lib. [ilegible]. cap. 7.) here and beyond Seas in Henry the eighths time, touching his marriage with his brother Arthurs widow, by Papall dispensation. The King had first a scruple cast into his mind about it by the Bishop of Baion the French Embassadour, who came to him to consult of a Marriage between the Lady Mary, and the Duke of Orleans, whether Mary were legitimate, &c. This gave occasion to the casting the Popes authority out of England. Mary was forced, for fear of death, to renounce the Bishop of Rome, and to acknowledge (Camdens Elisab. Introd.) her Mothers marriage to have bin incestuous and unjust, &c. Though afterwards, she set up the Pope here again: and it was her policy, so to get, and keep the Crown upon [ilegible] head.

And for all the evills, which Herod, &c.] John reproved him with the same liberty that Herod committed them. So did John Chrysostome, ([ilegible]. Hist. [ilegible]. Cent. 5. [ilegible]. 1. cap. 6.) the great ones of his time. Ità quidem ut etiam Ducum, Eutropii & Gainae, imò ipsius Imperatoris errata reprehenderet: He spared not Dukes, Princes, nay not the Emperour himself.

entries.title: Luke 3:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: There is no stint in sin: but as one wedge makes way for another: so here. As after Jonathan and [ilegible] Armour-bearer, came the whole host: So.

entries.title: Luke 3:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Prayer is the key of Gods Kingdom: And must be used, as at other times, so especially when we or ours receive the Sacraments: though the most, if urged hereto, must say, if they say truely as 1 Sam. 17. 39. I cannot go with these accoutrements: for I am not accustomed to them.

entries.title: Luke 3:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
But falsly: for Joseph was no more then his Pater politicus, as Postellus calleth him his foster-father, reputed father.

Which was the sonne of Heli] That is, his son in law. For Heli was Maries naturall father: and it is Maries genealogy that is here (So Ruth 1. 11, 12, 13.) described: but put upon Joseph, because the Hebrewes reckon not their genealogies by women, but by men only.

entries.title: Luke 3:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Salathiel was naturally the son of Neri, but legally, and by succession the son of Jechoniah, Matt. 4. 12. for he succeeded him in the Kingdom. Neri which signifieth My candle, seemeth to have bin so named from the candle which the Lord reserved for David and his house, 2 Chron. 21. 7.

entries.title: Luke 3:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Our Saviours genealogy is here the more accurately described, because there were that would have substituted and put false Christs upon the Church Ezek. 2. 62. The Preists that could not produce their genealogies were outed.

entries.title: Luke 3:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This name crept by (Bez. in loc. Pareus in Gen. 11) some meanes, into the Greek copies after Jeromies time, saith Beza and [ilegible]. Others say, that Saint Luke herein followed the Septuagints translation, out of wisdom and charity to the Hellenists (Alsted. Chron.) or Greek-Jewes, that had received it, and read it. 2. That (M. Lightfoots [ilegible]. p. 312.) writing for heathens, he followed the heathens Bible in his quotations. 3. That in his genealogies he was to be a Coppier, not a Corector.

entries.title: Luke 3:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not by generation, but creation. Therefore the Syriack translatour hath it Demen Elaba, A Deo, Of God, not Bar Elaha, the son of God.

entries.title: Luke 4:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: NO sooner out of the water of baptisme, but in the fire of temptation. After greatest feelings, we are to expect sharpest assaults: neither can we better quench the Devils fiery darts then with the water of baptisme. We read, saith Luther, of a certain holy virgin, who, whensoever sollicited to sin, would stop the tempters mouth with this one answer Christiana sum, I am a Christian. Intellexit enim hostis statim virtutem Baptismi & fidei —. & fugit ab ea. Satan could not abide the mentions of baptisme, but fled from her presently.

entries.title: Luke 4:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: During which time, he was set upon with al sorts of temptations. These three here recorded were likely the very worst; in quibus Diabolus omnes astus & [ilegible] suae sacculos deplevit, (as one saith) wherein the Devill did his utmost.

entries.title: Luke 4:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bread of deceit is sweet to a (Prov. 20. 17.) man, but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravell. Compare this verse with verse 9. and see how the devill usually tempteth by extreams, to make men offend either in defect, or excesse. Thus he tempted Master Knox upon his death-bed, if not to despair, ([ilegible].) then to presume that heaven should be his, for his zeal in the Scottish Reformation.

entries.title: Luke 4:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In visible landskip of his own making, presented to the eye.

entries.title: Luke 4:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Pope, as heir to the Devill, takes upon him to be Dominus regnorum mundi. Boniface. 8. wrote to Philip King of France, that he was lord of all, both Temporals and Spirituals, in all countries. Os papae & cultus diabobi in eodem sunt praedicamento, saith one. But, Cui volo do illa, is Gods only to say Dan. 4. Z 2.

entries.title: Luke 4:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Papa duliâ adorandus, say the Canonists.

entries.title: Luke 4:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matthew 4. 10.

entries.title: Luke 4:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: We must look for the tother bout, and in a calm prepare for a storm. The tempter is restlesse and impudent: so that a man is to expect, if he live out his dayes, to be urged to all sins, to the breach of every branch of the ten commandements, and to be put to it in respect of every Article of the Creed.

entries.title: Luke 4:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Without which the word is preached to no purpose. Cathedram in caelo habet, qui corda docer, saith Augustine. It is with the word and spirit, as with the veines and arteries; as the veines carry the bloud, so the arteries carry the spirits to quicken the bloud.

entries.title: Luke 4:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Envy it self was thrattled, which yet usually waits upon vertue. Every Zopyrus hath his Zoilus.

entries.title: Luke 4:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
The Jewes were to be kind to the AEgyptians, and to pray for the prosperity of Babylon, where they had bin bred, and fed. Be ye thankfull, Coloss. 3. 15, viz. to your friends and benefactors.

And stood up for to read] In honour of the word that he read: So [ilegible]. 8. 5. A commendable custome.

entries.title: Luke 4:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Whether he looked for it, or it so fell out by a providence, its uncertain. Origen, after his fall, lighting on that text, Psal. 50. What hast thou to do to take my words, &c. fell into a passion of weeping, and came out of the pulpit, as not able to speak to the people. Augustine hearing from heaven Tolle, lege, and happening upon that place Rom. 13. 14. Put (Aug. Confess. lib. 8 cap. 12.) ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, &c. was presently converted thereby. So was Cyprian, by reading the prophecy of Jonah.

entries.title: Luke 4:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Therefore the Gospel is a sure saying, and worthy of al acceptation, sith its an effect of the holy Spirit: doubt not of its excellency, authority, certainty, sufficiency. See my True Treasure.

entries.title: Luke 4:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A joyfull Jubilee. Let us not stand out the time, least we be bored in the eare by the Devill.

entries.title: Luke 4:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A good help against distractions. Our hearts are fickle and fugitive, if not hard held to it.

entries.title: Luke 4:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This was the summe of his sermon, as were also the [ilegible] we read, the heads only and short notes of the Prophets larger discourses. Brevity breeds obscurity.

entries.title: Luke 4:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And what of that? But it is still the course of our hearers, to look round about, if possibly they may find any hole in our coat, through which to flight and slip the coards of our doctrine, though they cannot but admire it.

entries.title: Luke 4:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is thy Country. So that for a man to cure his Country, is to cure himself.

entries.title: Luke 4:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matt. 13. 57.

entries.title: Luke 4:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. God hath [ilegible] on whom he will have mercy, &c. He is a free agent, and may do with his own as he pleaseth. If the Prophets, by the Spirits direction, healed and helped forraigners sooner then Israelites; what so great wonder that Christ did not that for his own Country, that he did for others?

entries.title: Luke 4:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A calamitous name, 2 Sam. 14. 5. The Hebrewes call her Almanah, a dumb woman, because either she dare not, or may not speak for her self: but God professeth himself the patron of such; and he can speak for them in the hearts of their greatest adversaries. Happy they in such an Advocate.

entries.title: Luke 4:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Nor he neither so long as he looked upon Gods Jordan with Syrian eyes.

entries.title: Luke 4:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Though but plain rusticks, yet they soon understood this saying of preaching to the Gentiles: which put them into an anger, and our Saviour into a danger.

entries.title: Luke 4:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As unworthy to tread on their pavement. And so mad they were, that they could neither stay till the businesse were brought to a judiciall tryall, nor forbear execution till the Sabbath were over.

entries.title: Luke 4:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Like a second Sampson: [ilegible] own arme saved him. This might have convinced his adversaries; but that they were mad with malice.

entries.title: Luke 4:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Contempt drives away Christ. And woe be unto you if I forsake you, Hos. 9. 12. Contend earnestly for the Faith, sith it is but once delivered to the Saints, Jude 3. You must never expect another edition of it.

entries.title: Luke 4:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He preached not frigide & trepidè, as the Scribes: but uttered oracles, and did miracles.

entries.title: Luke 4:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See Notes on Mark 1. 23.

entries.title: Luke 4:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Pope will needs be called Most Holy: and so lifts up himself above Christ.

entries.title: Luke 5:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: THis was both an argument of the truth of his humanity (that he was throng'd and thrust [ilegible] by the unmannerly multitude) and a part of his passion.

entries.title: Luke 5:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Though they laboured last night and had taken nothing. Ferendum & sperandum. Hope beguiles calamity, as good company doth the way.

entries.title: Luke 5:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Gr. He gently asked him, Will you ([ilegible]) be pleased to thrust out a little? See Philem. 8, 9. Posse & nolle, [ilegible] est.

Taught the people out of the ship] Any place served him for a pulpit. So if men be desirous to hear, they will make a mat a seat, a pair of legs a [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 5:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This is the fare he paies them, for the use of their ship. No man [ilegible] by Christ.

entries.title: Luke 5:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Omnia fui, & nihil expedit, (Spartian.) said Severus the Emperour. See Hab. 2. 13. Hag. 2. 6. If God stop not that hole in the bottom of the bag, all will run [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 5:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yet the [ilegible] got not out: which some note for another miracle.

entries.title: Luke 5:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Here the dumb fishes do cleerly preach Christ to be the Son of God.

entries.title: Luke 5:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. A man, a sinner, a ([ilegible]) very mixture and compound of dirt and sin. See the like phrase, Numb. 32. 14.

entries.title: Luke 5:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Fear seazed upon him, ([ilegible]) and surrounded him, as Tacitus saith Induere pavores.

entries.title: Luke 5:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matthew 4. 19.

entries.title: Luke 5:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They had given their names to him before, John 1. But now they see by this miracle his power to provide for them, they leave all to live with him. We love to see how we shall subsist.

entries.title: Luke 5:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It is a ready way to speed, to found our prayers upon the power of God.

entries.title: Luke 5:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So ready is Christ to gratifie his suppliants, yea to be commanded by them, Isaiah 45. 11.

entries.title: Luke 5:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For a Bill of Indictment against them. Reprobates shall give an heavy account to God of all the means and offers of grace.

entries.title: Luke 5:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Fame followes them that fly from it, and the contrary: as the Crocodile doth.

entries.title: Luke 5:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Pray, if you meane to prosper.

entries.title: Luke 5:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So tis, when any Ordinance is afoot.

entries.title: Luke 5:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on [ilegible]. 8. 2, 3, &c. and on Mark 2. 3. &c.

entries.title: Luke 5:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Let our sicknesses mind us of our sins, that we may soon seek pardon.

entries.title: Luke 5:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. Neither of either: for both are equally hard, and feisable to God alone.

entries.title: Luke 5:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: [ilegible] Paradoxes, things that we ([ilegible].) never thought to have seen: and above beleif, had we not seen them.

entries.title: Luke 5:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This is fulfilled saith Bellarmine, in our Lent-fasts. But this was fulfilled say we, [ilegible] ([ilegible]. de [ilegible] cap. 10.) Christ was crucified, and the Apostles mourned. Papists set-fasts are meer mock-fasts.

entries.title: Luke 5:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, milder, and so pleasanter. Vetustate enim vina mitescunt, quia vetustas igneum calorem, acerbitatem, & [ilegible] e vino tollit. Age clarifies wine, and ripens ([ilegible].) it.

entries.title: Luke 6:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: JErom saith, that he asked Nazianzen what this second Sabbath ([ilegible].) after the first was? Nazianzen answered, I'le tell you that, when I come next into the pulpit, for there you cannot contradict me. It a perjocum dixit (saith Melanchthon) quod hodie serio [ilegible]. See the Note on Matt. 12. 1.

entries.title: Luke 6:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Our Saviour grants that it had not been lawfull indeed, but in case of hard hunger.

entries.title: Luke 6:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yes, over and over: but either understood not, or, through malice, dissembled it. Quilibet nostrum de lege interrogatus facilus quam nomen suum respondet, saith Josephus. The Jewes were all very wel versed in the Scriptures.

entries.title: Luke 6:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matthew 12. 9, 10, 11, &c.

entries.title: Luke 6:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He premiseth prayer being to make choise of the twelve. If Eleazar prayed when to seek a wife for Isaac, Gen. 24. If Salomon prayed for wisdom, ere he set upon the Temple-work. If Ezra fasted and prayed, ere he committed the golden and silver vessels to them that kept them, Ezra 8. 21. 30. Should there not prayer be made for Ministers, ere they be set over Gods house and people?

entries.title: Luke 6:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See Notes on Matthew [ilegible]. 1.

entries.title: Luke 6:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Here we have a repetition of that famous Sermon in the Mount, Matt. 5. 6, 7. See the Notes there.

entries.title: Luke 6:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ubicunque invenitur [ilegible] Calvini, deleatur, saith the Index expurgatorius. Persecutors proscribe true professours, tanquam nequissimos & lucis hujus usurâ indignos. After Joh. Husse was burnt, his adversaries got his heart which was left untoucht by the fire, and beat it with their staves. (Epist. [ilegible]. 16. ad [ilegible].) A Frier preaching to the people at Antwerp, wished that Luther were there, that he might bite out his throat with his teeth, as Erasmus testifieth.

entries.title: Luke 6:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Worldlings jollity is but as a Book fairly bound: which, when its opened, is full of [ilegible] but tragedies.

entries.title: Luke 6:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: What evill have I done said Aristides, when one told him he had every mans good (Sen. de [ilegible]. [ilegible].) word? Male de me loquuntur; sed mali saith Seneca. Malis [ilegible], [ilegible] est. When Doeg blasted David, he thinks the better of himself, Psal. 52. 8. Latymer sayes, he was glad when any (Serm last afore King Edward.) objected indiscretion against him in his Sermons: for by that, he knew the matter was good; else they would soon have condemned that.

entries.title: Luke 6:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Socrates, when one gave him a box on the ear in the market-place said, Quam molestum est nescire homines quando prodire debeant cum galea? What an odde thing it is to go abroad without a head-peice.

entries.title: Luke 6:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Generall Norrice never thought he had that, that he gave not away. It is not lack, but love of mony that maketh men churles.

Ask them not again] Or if thou take the benefit of the Law to recover them, do it without hate or heat: as Tilters break their spears on each others breasts, yet without wrath, or intention of hurt.

entries.title: Luke 6:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The most part ([ilegible] [ilegible] Travels.) of the Turks Civill Justice is grounded upon this Rule as is above noted.

entries.title: Luke 6:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
No not the principall, in case thy brother be not able to repay it. Thomas Tomkins Martyr a Weaver dwelling in Shore-ditch, whensoever any had come to borrow mony of him, would shew them such mony as he had in (Acts and Mon. [ilegible]. [ilegible].) his purse, and bid them take it: And when they came to repay it again, so far was he from Usury, that he would bid them keep it longer, till they were better able.

To the unthankfull, and to the evill] An unthankfull man is a naughty man: nay, he is an ugly man, Psal. 147. 1.

entries.title: Luke 6:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Jewes ware large and loose garments, so that they could bare away much in their bosomes. Hence this expression.

entries.title: Luke 7:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: PIscator thinks that this History is not the same with that Matthew 8. 5. His reasons may be read in his Scholia on that place. Videsis.

entries.title: Luke 7:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So they held him: but he held himself unworthy, vers. 6. God in like manner saith that Jerusalem had received double for her sinnes, Isaiah 40. 2. But Jerusalem her self saith, Our God hath punished us lesse then our sins, Ezra 9. 13. Too much, saith God: Too little, saith she: and yet how sweetly and beautifully doth this kind of contradiction become both?

entries.title: Luke 7:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Antiochus had burnt up the Synagogues in sundry places. This man, now converted, is content to be at cost for God and his people. So the Israelites received to favour again after their foul fall in setting up the golden calf, brought enough and to spare toward the work of the Tabernacle.

entries.title: Luke 7:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So saith Jacob of himself, Gen. 32. 10. so Paul, 1 Cor. 15. so the Baptist. Matt. 3. so Augustine, Non sum dignus, quem tu diligas, Domine, I am not worthy of thy love, Lord.

entries.title: Luke 7:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matt. 8. 10.

entries.title: Luke 7:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Though a young man. Our decrepit age both expects death and sollicits it: but vigorous youth lookes strangly upon that grim sergeant of God. Senibus mors in jannis, adolescentibus in insidiis, Bern. Death seizeth on old men, and layes wait for the youngest.

entries.title: Luke 7:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of his own free accord, and unrequested, he raised him. Christ had a most tender heart. How shall he not pity and provide for his praying people?

entries.title: Luke 7:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The soul resteth not till it pitch upon Christ. See the Notes on Matt. 11. 2. &c.

entries.title: Luke 7:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This is check to them for their preposterous zeal for John, their Master. Therefore also our Saviour commends not John, till they were departed.

entries.title: Luke 7:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This is no small comfort to the Ministers of the Gospel, against the contempts cast upon them by the world. They are some-bodies in heaven, what ever men make of them.

entries.title: Luke 7:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: i. e. They glorified his word, Act. 13. 48. and acknowledged his righteousnesse, repenting of their sins, and beleeving Johns and Christs testimony, which the Pharisees so pertinaciously rejected.

entries.title: Luke 7:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Being ingrati gratiae Dei, as Ambrose speaketh, and so much the further off, for that they saw the people so forward.

entries.title: Luke 7:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But Locusts and wild Hony.

entries.title: Luke 7:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, her disciples, Psal. 34. 11.

entries.title: Luke 7:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It was fit he should feast sometimes, that fared so hard mostly.

entries.title: Luke 7:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
They that make their eyes a fountain to wash Christs feet in, shall have his side for a fountain, to wash their souls in.

Kissed his feet] But how many now refuse those kisses of his mouth, Cant. c. 1. by despising the word preached, that sweet pledge of his love?

entries.title: Luke 7:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
See the picture of an hypocrite, slighting and censuring his betters.

What manner of woman this is] Syr. What an ill name she hath, for a light huswife.

entries.title: Luke 7:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He that receives a curtesie, we say, sells his liberty. But so did not Christ at Simons, at Martha's, &c. table. His mouth was not stopped with good chear. He entertains the Pharisees with as many menaces, as they do him with messes of meat.

entries.title: Luke 7:44
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: We read not that the Virgin Mary ever did as this greater sinner did. Repentance is the fair child of that foul mother, sin, as the Romane said of Pompey. ([ilegible].) And it is question whether more glorifies God, Innocence or Penitence?

entries.title: Luke 7:47
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Nam, notificativum est, non impulsivum. Her love was an Argument (not a cause) that her sins were forgiven her.

entries.title: Luke 7:48
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Melanchthon makes mention of a godly woman, who having upon her death-bed been much conflicted, and afterwards much comforted, brake out into these words; Now, and not till now, I understand the meaning of those words, Thy sins are forgiven. It is storied of another that courting a curtezan, and understanding that her name was Mary: he remembred Mary Magdelen, and forbearing to commit that act of filthinesse that he intended, became a sound convert.

entries.title: Luke 8:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: EXodus 31. After sicknesse, they were to offer to God the ransome of their lives. Hezekiah testified his thankfulnesse for recovery, by a song: these good women, by following Christ; when they might have staied at home with more ease to themselves; and more thank of their friends. Nay, very Heathens after a fit of sicknesse, would consecrate something to their gods.

entries.title: Luke 8:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or Treasurer, as the Arabick calleth him: his Vicar-Generall, or Protetrach.
