This Court-Lady followeth Christ: so did Serena the Empresse, who was therefore Martyred by her husband Diocletian. So Elizabeth (Luth, in Epist. ad Jo. Agricol.) Queen of Denmark; of whom Luther testifieth, that she died a faithfull professour of the Reformed Religion: and addeth, Scilicet Christus etiam aliquando voluit Reginam in coelum vehere. Christ would once save a Queen; which he doth not often.

entries.title: Luke 8:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on [ilegible]. 13. 2, 3, &c.

entries.title: Luke 8:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Least, if it should lie long (Jam. 1. 21.) upon their hard hearts, it should break through them with its weight, as being able to save their souls.

entries.title: Luke 8:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Viz. About their worldly businesses; which as the lean kine in Pharaohs dreame, devour the fat, and it is nothing seen by them. After a while, they remember no more then the man in the Moon doth, what they had heard delivered.

entries.title: Luke 8:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Referred to the end, and intent in the action.

And good heart] In respect of inward renewed qualities.

Having heard the word, keep it] As food or physick, which if not kept, profiteth not. They incorporate it into their souls, so as it becomes an ingrafted word; they are transformed into the same image, conformed to the heavenly patterne.

With patience] Or, with tarriance for the fit season: Not as ([ilegible].) that rath-ripe fruit, vers. 13. and Psal. 129.

entries.title: Luke 8:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. Though to you it is given to know Mysteries, &c. as verse 10. yet not for your owne use onely, but that your light may shine before men.

entries.title: Luke 8:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For else ye shall neither bear good fruits, nor be born with for your barrennesse. All shall out, and you shall smart for it.

entries.title: Luke 8:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It is not the having faith, but the living by it, the actuating of it, that helps us in an exigence.

entries.title: Luke 8:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All Pharaohs cruelty exercised over the Israelites, was nothing to this. Oh then (Chrysost.) the unexpressible torments of the damned! Utinam ubique de Gehenna dissereretur! saith a Father. I could wish men would discourse much and oft of hell.

entries.title: Luke 8:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As a horse is by his ([ilegible].) rider (so the word signifieth) or a ship with oares. All wicked men are acted and agitated by the devill, Eph. 2. 2. Persecutors especially. (Bern.) Quod si videris aliquando persecutorem tuum nimis saevientem, scito quia ab ascensore suo Diabolo perurgetur. If Persecutors sometimes be more moderate, it is because the devill spurs not so hard.

entries.title: Luke 8:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: We must be ready and well appointed to resist: for the devil sets upon us not without military discipline, and singular skill, Cataphractus incedit Satan, saith Luther. The devill marcheth well armed and in good array.

entries.title: Luke 8:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So would the possessed man soon have done, but that God preserved him.

entries.title: Luke 8:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As fearing, least if he departed, he should be repossessed. So we see its an old error and weaknesse for men to be too strongly conceited of Christs corporeall presence.

entries.title: Luke 9:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: PEndebat, animi dubius. He stood amused and amazed: he stuck in the mud, as it were, and could find no way out. This ([ilegible].) is the import of the Greek word. Thus the wicked, in the fulnesse of his sufficiency is in straits, as Zophar hath it, Job. 15. 22.

entries.title: Luke 9:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: with a faint and fruitlesse desire: for he never stirred out of doors to see Christ, though he beleived that God had raised him from the dead. So true is that of Abraham, Luke 16. 31. Perhaps he desired to see whether it were John or not.

entries.title: Luke 9:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Weary though he were, yet never weary of wel-doing.

entries.title: Luke 9:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Which is a thing not only improbable, but impossible. They held it an absurd motion.

entries.title: Luke 9:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Examinationi preces praemittendae. All our sacrifices should be salted with this salt.

entries.title: Luke 9:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This Pythagorean transanimation is held by the Jewes to this day, viz. (ut singuli tertio renascantur) against so many cleer testimonies of Scripture to the contrary.

entries.title: Luke 9:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Putting the two utmost dayes also into the reckoning. See the Notes on Matthew 17. 1. &c.

entries.title: Luke 9:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Dum ipsius mens tota Deose immergeret, (Luc. Burgens.) saith one. Christians, whiles they are praying are oft-times carried out and beyond themselves. See Matt. 17. 2, 3. and the Notes there.

entries.title: Luke 9:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Of his Exodus; in ([ilegible].) reference to that expedition or departute of Israel out of AEgypt. It signifieth a translating from a condition and state of hardship: and is also used by Saint Peter 2 Epistle 1. 15. Death to the Saints is but an out-going to heaven; a loosing from the shore of life, and (Philip. 1. 21.) launcing out into the maine of Immortality.

entries.title: Luke 9:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matthew 17. 5.

entries.title: Luke 9:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As in the falling sicknesse, it falls out.

entries.title: Luke 9:44
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ponite, reponite, lay ([ilegible].) up the sayings of my sufferings, notwithstanding this peoples vain applauses. The best balm cast into water, sinks to the bottom: the baser sort, flotes on the top.

entries.title: Luke 9:51
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
The word implies a ([ilegible] Poly. Lyser.) Metaphor from fathers owning and acknowledging their children after long absence.

He set his face] He steeled his forehead against all discouragements. ([ilegible])

entries.title: Luke 9:53
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Such is the hatred that Idolaters bear against all Gods true worshippers. Illam Domum in qua inventus fuerit haereticus diruendam decernimus: It was a Decree of the Counsell of Tholouse against the Albigenses.

entries.title: Luke 9:54
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
These two brethren, sons of thunder, how soon was their choler up? they had quick and hot spirits.

Wilt thou that we command] It were to be wished that we would first consult with Christ in his word, ere we stirre hand or foot to revenge.

entries.title: Luke 9:55
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
He did it not slightly, and by the by, but seriously and on set purpose: so must we rebuke and rebate our vindictive spirits, our unruly lusts, when like kine in a strait they rush and ride, one upon the back of another.

Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of] Not of Elias his spirit, as ye imagine: this wild-fire was never kindled on Gods hearth, as his zeal was: you are men of another mould then Elias. He was a Minister of indignation, you of consolation: his actions fit not you, because your persons are not like his: It is a ([ilegible] Arisiot.) rare thing to be of an heroicall Spirit saith the Moralist. Every man cannot be an Elias or a Phineas, Numb. 25. 8. To that height of heat, ordinary mens tempers ate not raised.

entries.title: Luke 9:58
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ had felt his pulse, and found his temper, that he looked after outward things only: and therefore he lets him know what to trust unto.

entries.title: Luke 9:62
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ here haply [ilegible] to that which Elisha did, 1 King 19. 19.

entries.title: Luke 10:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: AS his heralds, to foreshew his comming to Jerusalem, and to proclaime the true Jubilee.

entries.title: Luke 10:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Christ had no sooner bidden them pray, but he answers their prayers. When we bid our children ask us for this or that, it is because we mean to give it them.

As Lambs among Wolves] Sed sollicitudo pastoris boni efficit [ilegible] in agnos audere nil possint, saith Ambrose. The care of the good shepheard is the safety of the flock.

entries.title: Luke 10:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For that your task is long, your time is little.

entries.title: Luke 10:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not seeking after dainties. It becomes not a servant of the Highest, to be a slave to ([ilegible].) his palat. Epicurci, dum palato prospiciunt, coeli [ilegible] non suspiciunt, saith the heathen.

entries.title: Luke 10:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: There is in unbeleif an odious unthankfulnesse: Such judge themselves unworthy of eternall life, Act. 13. 44. they are condemned already, Joh. 3.

entries.title: Luke 10:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Julius [ilegible], complaining to the Emperour of wrong done to him by the Duke of Saxony, received this answer from him, Tuacausa erit meacausa: so saith Christ to all his servants. Causa ut sit magna, magnus est [ilegible] & author ejus: neque enim nostra est, saith Luther to [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 10:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: We are all naturally ambitious, and desirous of vain-glory. A small wind blowes up a bubble. Pray down this vanity.

entries.title: Luke 10:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, from mens hearts, which he accounts is heaven: but is cast out, by the mighty Gospel.

entries.title: Luke 10:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Mark 16. 18. Good Ministers tread so hard on the old Serpents head, that its no wonder he turns again, and nibbleth at their heeles.

entries.title: Luke 10:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That you are [ilegible] Burgesses of the new Jerusalem. Paul by his priviledge of being a Roman, escaped whipping: we by this escape [ilegible]. The sinner ingrosseth his name in the book of [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 10:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: With this prayer the Anabaptists (Scultet. Annal.) of Germany usually began their Sermons; thinking thereby to excuse their lack of learning. And then protested that they would deliver nothing but what was revealed to them from above.

entries.title: Luke 10:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: How blessed then are they that hear this Arch-prophet in heaven. Moses and Elias conversing with Christ in the Mount, could much better discourse of his decease, and other divine doctrines, then ever they could whiles here upon earth. An infant of one day there, is much beyond the deepest Doctor here.

entries.title: Luke 10:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Many righteous saith (Matth. 13. 17.) Matthew. Righteous persons are Kings.

entries.title: Luke 10:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Serviendum Deo toto (Martial.) corde: id est, amore summo, more vero, ore fideli, re omni: Hoc non fit verbis: Marce ut ameris, [ilegible].

Here some weak Christians are troubled, as conceiting that they love their children, friends, &c. better then God. But it is answered, 1. When two streames run in one channell (as here nature (D. Sibbes. on 1 Cor, 2. 9.) and grace do) they run stronger then one st eam doth. When a man loves God and the things of God, grace is alone: nature yeelds nothing to that. 2. We must not judge by an indeliberate passion. The love of God is a constant stream: not a torrent, but a current, that runs all our life time, but runs still and without (Claudian.) noyse, as the waters of Shiloh, and of Nilus, nullas confessus murmure vires, that runs smoothly.

With all thy strength] That is, saith a Divine, in our particular places. A Magistrate must execute Justice for Gods sake, &c.

entries.title: Luke 10:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Taking the tale out of his ([ilegible].) mouth, being ready with his answer. For he is that Palmoni Ham (Dan. 8. 13.) me dabbar in Daniel, that prime Prolocutour.

entries.title: Luke 10:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Indeed by the providence of God over ruling the matter, as it doth in things that to us are meerly casuall and contingent.

entries.title: Luke 10:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For fear of legall pollution. ([ilegible].) But two duties never meet so, as to crosse one another: the one of them yeilds: and the execution of the yeilding duty for the present hath reason of an offence. This Levites legall strictnesse was here a vice: he should rather have shewed mercy to his brother in misery. So that the Rule, Negatives alwayes bind, intends not that they are of an indispensable nature: but that every particular instant of time is to be observed for their obedience, (Huet of [ilegible]. page 175.) while and where they stand of force.

entries.title: Luke 10:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Turnebus [ilegible] putat Parabolanos, quasi aemulos Samaritani. Hoc autem nomine vocabantur, qui curandis debilium corporibus deputabantur. Those that looked to sick people were hence called Parabolanes, or Samaritans.

entries.title: Luke 10:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Wine to search, and Oyle to supple. Wine signifies the sharpnesse of the Law (saith Melanchthon) Oyle the sweetneste of the Gospel. Now, so great ([ilegible]. in [ilegible]. [ilegible]. Wigand. Syntag.) is the naturall sympathy and harmony between the vine and the olive, that the olive being grafted into the vine brings forth both grapes and olives.

entries.title: Luke 10:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As his disciples, Act. 22. 3. So the children of the Prophets of old: whence that expression, 2 King. 2. 3. Knowest thou not that the Lord will take away thy Master from thy head to day?

entries.title: Luke 10:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Diversly distracted. In ([ilegible].) multitude of worldly businesse, the soul is like a mill, where one cannot hear another, the noise is such as taketh away al entercourse. We should look at the world but only out at the eyes end as it were.

entries.title: Luke 10:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ prefers attention before attendance. To hearken is better then the fat of rammes, 1 Sam. 15. 22.

entries.title: Luke 10:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That bonum hominis, Mic. 6. 8. that totum hominis, Eccles. 12. 13. the happinesse, the whole of a man.

entries.title: Luke 11:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: OUr super-substantiall bread: so Erasmus rendreth it, and interpreteth ([ilegible].) it of Christ: for he thought that in so heavenly a prayer, there should have been no mention of earthly things; wherein he was greatly deceived. For temporals also must be pray'd for.

entries.title: Luke 11:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
So that our forgiving of others seemeth for Gods promise sake, to be as it were the intervenient cause, or the sine Qua non of Gods forgiving us, saith learned Beza.

And lead us not, &c.] One argument that we shall persevere, is, the prayers of the whole Church, offering up this daily sacrifice Lead us not, &c.

entries.title: Luke 11:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. His impudency: A ([ilegible].) metaphor from beggars, that will not be said; but are impudently importunate.

entries.title: Luke 11:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ask, seek, knock. It is not a simple repetition of the same thing, but an emphaticall gradation, and shewes instantissimam necessitatem, saith Augustine. Nec dicitur quid dabitur, saith he, to shew that the gift is a thing supra [ilegible] nomen, above all name.

entries.title: Luke 11:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Sozomen saith of Apollonius, that he never asked any thing of God that he obtained not. Hic homo potuit apud Deum quod voluit, said one concerning Luther. He could have what he would of God.

entries.title: Luke 11:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So it was a double miracle: Gods favours seldome come single: there is a series, a concatenation of them, and every former drawes on a future.

entries.title: Luke 11:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Qui se dedebant, arma tradebant. Caesar de bell. Gall. lib. 3. They that yeilded threw down their arms.

entries.title: Luke 11:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: His only rest is to molest and mischeif men.

entries.title: Luke 11:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As the Jaylour layes load of iron on him that had escaped. None are worse then those that have been good, and are naught: and might be good, but will be naught.

entries.title: Luke 11:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: His disciples were more blessed in hearing Christ, then his mother in bearing him.

entries.title: Luke 11:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All on a heape, ([ilegible]) either to see a signe, or to heare what hee would say to the motion.

entries.title: Luke 11:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Our Saviour here warneth those that had given some good hope of their Repentance, that they cherish their light, and walke by it.

entries.title: Luke 11:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A single eye, is that that looks on God singly, abstracted from all other things.

entries.title: Luke 11:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And yet, at their own tables, he sets the Pharisees forth in their colours, and entertaineth them with as many menaces as they do him with messes of meat.

entries.title: Luke 11:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This the Pharisees deemed ([ilegible]. Antiq. Heb. 49.) as great a sin as to commit fornication.

entries.title: Luke 11:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
So Daniel counsels [ilegible], Chap. 4. 27.

Of such things as ye have] Gr. As are within: either within ([ilegible]) the platter (send morsels to the hungry) or within your hearts: for riches get within their owners many times, and do more possesse them, then are possessed by them; —difficile est opibus non tradere mentem.

entries.title: Luke 11:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Notwithstanding your tything of pot-herbs; wherein you think you take course that all things may be clean to you, vers. 41. Or woe unto you, for that through covetousnesse you exact the utmost of your tithes, &c. So some sense this text.

entries.title: Luke 11:44
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As the deep grave keeps the stinking carkasse from offending any ones smell: so doth the dissembling hypocrite so cleanly carry the matter that hardly the sharpest nose, &c.

entries.title: Luke 11:45
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who meddled with them but that their own consciences accused them? It is a rule of Jerome, Ubi generalis de vitiis disputatio est, ibi nullius personae est injuria: neque carbone notatur quisquam, quasi malus sit, sed omnes admonentur ne sint mali. Where the discourse is of all, there's no personall intimation of any.

entries.title: Luke 11:48
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And so ye set up the trophies of your fathers cruelty.

entries.title: Luke 11:49
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, Christ himself, the essentiall wisdome of his Father, Matthew 23. 34.

entries.title: Luke 11:52
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
I see well, said Father Latimer, (Acts. and Mon. fol. 1590.) that whosoever will be busy with Vaevobis, he shall shortly after come coram nobis, as Christ did.

For ye have taken away the key of knowledge] By taking away the Scriptures, and all good meanes of knowledge: as do also the Jesuites at this day. At Dole, an University in Burgundy, they have not only debarred the people of the Protestant books, but especially also forbid them to talk of God, either in good sort or bad. In Italy they not only prohibit the books of the Reformed writers, but also hide their own Treatises, in which the Tenet of the Protestants is recited, only to be confuted: so that you shall seldome there meet with Bellarmines works, or any of the like nature to be sold.

entries.title: Luke 11:53
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Out of deep displeasure ([ilegible]) to bear an aking tooth towards him (as Herodias did toward the Baptist, Mark 6. 19.) waiting him a shrewd turn.

And to provoke him to speake] Not to stop his mouth about many things, as the Rhemists falsly render it. They asked him captious ([ilegible]) questions, to make him an offendour for a word, Isaiah 29. 21.

entries.title: Luke 12:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: WHich our eyes cannot discern from dough by the colour; but only our palate, by the taste. Such is hypocrisie; which also, as leaven, is 1 spreading: 2 swelling: 3 sowring the meal: 4 impuring aud defiling the house where it is, though it be but as much as a mans fist.

entries.title: Luke 12:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matt. 10. 19. and on Mark [ilegible]. 11. Alice Driver Martyr, at her examination, put all the Doctors to silence, so that they had not a word to say, but one looked upon another. Then she said, Have ye no more to say? God be honoured: you be not able to resist the Spirit of God in me a poor woman I was an honest poor mans daughter, never brought up in the University, as you have been. But I have driven the Plough many a time before my father, I thank God: yet notwithstanding in the defence of Gods Truth, and in the cause ([ilegible] & [ilegible]. [ilegible].) of my Master Christ, by his grace I will set my foot against the foot of any of you all, in the maintenance and defence of the same: And if I had a thousand lives, it should go for payment thereof: So the Chancellour condemned her, and she returned to the [ilegible], as joyfull, as the bird of day.

entries.title: Luke 12:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This our [ilegible] addes after who made me a Judge? to teach us not to go to Law with a covetous mind: but as Charles the French King made War with our Henry the Seventh, more desiring peace then victory.

For a [ilegible] life consisteth not, &c.] He can neither live upon them, nor lengthen his life by them. Queen Elizabeth once wished her self a milk-maid: Bajazet envied the happinesse of a poor shepheard that sate on a hill-side merrily reposing himself with his homely pipe: Therein shewing, saith the historian, that worldly ([ilegible]. hist 216) blisse consisteth not so much in possessing of much, subject to danger, as in joying in a little contentment void of fear.

entries.title: Luke 12:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. The country: ([ilegible].) for he had laid field to field, till he was the only land-holder thereabouts; and had a country of corn, Esay 58.

entries.title: Luke 12:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
He was up with the more, and down with the lesse: he cast up his reckonings, as covetous mens manner is, and after long debate to and fro, concluded what to do.

He talked to himself, &c.] A marvelous proper word for the ([ilegible]) purpose.

entries.title: Luke 12:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A right Epicure, one that had made his gut his God: another Sardanapalus, that did eate that in earth, that he disgested in hell, as Augustine hath it.

entries.title: Luke 12:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This rich foole when, like a Jay, he was pruning himself in the boughs, came tumbling down with the arrow in his side: his glasse was run, when he thought it to be but new turned. He chopt into the earth before he was aware: like as one, that walking in a field cover'd with snow, falleth into a pit suddenly. He was shot as a bird with a bolt whilst he gazed at the bow: And this may be any mans case. Which made Austin say he would not for the gain of a world be an Atheist for one half hour: because he knew not but God might in that time call him.

Then whose shall those things be, &c.?] As thy friends are scrambling for thy goods, worms for thy body, so devils for thy soul. We read of Henry Beauford that rich and wretched Cardinall, Bishop of Winchester, and Chancellour of England in the reign of King Henry the Sixth, that perceiving he must needs die, he murmur'd that his riches could not repreive him. Fie, quoth he, (Fox Martyrol. vol. 1. pag 925.) will not Death be hired? will mony do nothing? No: its righteousnesse only that delivereth from death.

entries.title: Luke 12:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For superfluities, when ye cannot provide your selves of necessaries?

entries.title: Luke 12:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hang not in suspence, ([ilegible].) as meteors doe in the ayre, not certaine whether to hang or fall to the ground, Meteoradicta volunt quod animos hominum (Magir. Physic.) suspensos, dubios, et quasi fluctuantes faciant. Aristotle himselfe confesseth, that of some meteors he knew not what to say, though of some other he could say somewhat. One Interpreter renders this word, Make not discourses in the ayre, as the covetous man doth, when his head is tossed with the cares of getting, or feares of losing commodity; Or it may note his endlesse framing of projects for the compassing of his desires. The Syriack rendreth it, Let not your thoughts be distracted about these things. Surely as a clock can never stand still, so long as the plummets hang thereat: so neither can a worldlings heart, for cares and anxieties. These suffer him not to rest night or day; being herein like unto the flyes of Egypt, or those tyrants Esay 16.

entries.title: Luke 12:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr: Little, little flock. There is in the originall a double diminutive. If we divide the known parts of the world into three equall Parts, the Christians part is but (Breerw. Enqui. pag. 118.) as five, the Mahometans as sixe, and the Idolaters as nineteene. Among the best Churches the most are the worst, as, Philip 3. 18. Chrysostome could not find an hundred in Antioch, that he could be well perswaded of that they should be saved.

entries.title: Luke 12:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As a merchant being to travell into a farre countrey, doth deliver his money here upon the [ilegible], that so he may be sure to receive it againe at his arrivall in that Countrey: so let us that are passing into another Country, lay up something that may stand us in stead in that day.

entries.title: Luke 12:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: your inwardest affection, your [ilegible] joy and trust.

entries.title: Luke 12:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It implyes 1. Readinesse 2. Nimblenesse, handinesse and handsomenesse. A loose, discinct and diffluent mind is unfit to serve God. Here it is, ungirt, unblest.

entries.title: Luke 12:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So verse 38. and 43. They are three times said to be blessed that watch, Terque quaterque beati: ([ilegible].) Faelices ter et [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 12:47
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: None are so filled with Gods wrath, as knowing men. Sapientes sapienter descendunt in [ilegible], saith Bernard. The Devill is too hard for them.

entries.title: Luke 12:48
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To know our masters will is the great ([ilegible].) talent of all o her. There is a [Much] in that, There is a speciall ([ilegible] [ilegible].) depositum, as the word here used importeth.

entries.title: Luke 12:49
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, that persecution (1 Tim. 6. 20.) (1 Tim. 1. 14.) that is Evangelii genius, as Calvin wrote to the French King, and dogges at the heeles the preaching of the truth.

entries.title: Luke 12:50
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This painfull preconceit of his passion, was a part of our Saviours passion. This made him spend many a night in prayer, bewayling our sins, and imploring Gods grace, and he was heard in that which he requested, Heb. 5.

entries.title: Luke 12:57
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By consulting with your owne consciences, which would, if rightly dealt with, tell you, that I am that Messias you have so long look't for.

entries.title: Luke 12:58
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Purus putus [ilegible], saith Drusius. ([ilegible].) Da operam: Id est, festina, & labora, omnesque [ilegible] cogita quomodo ab eo libereris, as Theophylact expounds it. Be at utmost paines to get freed from him.

entries.title: Luke 12:59
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It is good to compound quickly with the Lord, and to take up the suite before it come to execution and judgement, lest we be forced to pay not onely the main debt, but the arrearages too, that is the time of Gods long-suffering and patience, here and [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 13:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: SO called from Judas Gaulonites or Galilaeus their Captaine: to whose faction also belonged those foure thousand murderers Act. 21. 38. For Pilate had not authority over the Galileans properly so called. See Ioseph. lib. 18. cap. 2.

entries.title: Luke 13:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: None out of hell ever suffered more then those worthyes Heb. 11. Shall any therefore condemne that generation of [ilegible] children Psal. 73. 15? See [ilegible]. 4. 6. Dan. 9. 12.

entries.title: Luke 13:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: [ilegible] aut pereundum. Men must either turne from sinne, or burne in hell.

entries.title: Luke 13:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Except the best of you all repent more and more, when yee see the examples of Gods wrath, &c. God would not have the wounds of godly sorrow so healed up in his owne children, but that they should bleed afresh upon every good occasion, [ilegible] plagis [ilegible] medicamenta [ilegible]. Make best use of others miseries.

entries.title: Luke 13:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Trees that are not for fruit are for the fire. God will lay downe his basket, and take up his axe. He will not alwayes serve men for a sinning-stock.

entries.title: Luke 13:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Happy that people, that have praying vine-dressers to intercede for them! God will yeeld somewhat to prayer, when he is bitterly bent against a people or person.

Till I shall dig, &c.] Donec eam ablaqueavero & stercot [ilegible]. ([ilegible].) Ministers must try their utmost to fulfill their ministery that they have received of the Lord. Colos. 4. 17.

entries.title: Luke 13:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Syriaek rendreth it Assumens vultum, Thou that [ilegible] a good face upon it, thou that personatest a better man then thou art; thou picture of piety, &c.

entries.title: Luke 13:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Few received Christ in the [ilegible] [ilegible]. 1. 12. [ilegible] wondred at one good [ilegible]. They are [ilegible] that look [ilegible]. [ilegible] in [ilegible]. The most [ilegible] on that old popish rule, to follow [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 13:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Strive even to an agony; or as they ([ilegible].) did for the garland in the Olympick games, to the which the word here used seemeth to allude. All would come to heaven, but all like not the way; they would not per angusta ad augusta pervenire: they like well of Abrahams bosome, but not of Dives his doore. But let none think to live in Dalilahs lap, and then to rest in Abraham; bosome, to dance with the Devill all day, and then to [ilegible] with Christ at night; to fly to heaven with pleasant wings, to passe a deliciis ad delicias, e coeno ad coelum, &c. to goe to heaven in a feather-bed.

entries.title: Luke 13:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: These pretenders to Christ perish by catching at their owne catch, hanging on their owne fancy, making a bridge of their owne shadow, &c. they verily beleeve that Christ is their sweet Saviour, &c. when it's no such matter: they trust to Christ, as the Apricock tree that leanes against the wall, but is fast rooted in the earth, so are these in the world, &c.

entries.title: Luke 13:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As at a sumptuous supper. When therefore we are invited to a full feast, think of heaven: As Fulgentius beholding at Rome the Majesty of the Emperour, the glory of the Senate, the lustre of the Nobility, cryed out, How beautifull is Jerusalem the Caelestiall, sith Rome the Terrestriall appeareth with such splendor? So Master Esty when he sate and heard a (D. Hall's Art of div. Medit.) sweet consort of Musick, seemed upon this occasion carried up for the time before-hand to the place of his rest, saying very passionately, What Musick may we think there is in heaven?

entries.title: Luke 13:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
i. e. As long as I list, without his leave. Faith makes a man walk about the world as a conquerour.

I shall be perfected] Or, I shall be sacrificed, as [ilegible] rendreth ([ilegible] In [ilegible].) it.

entries.title: Luke 14:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: GRaece, They superstitiously and maliciously observed him. Aristot. ([ilegible]) lib. 2. Rhetor. accipit pro eo quod est ulciscendi [ilegible] captare. They watched as intently as a dog doth for a bone: they pryed as narrowly into his actions, as Laban did into Jacobs stuffe.

entries.title: Luke 14:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A fit object, and that was sufficient to move him to mercy, who himself, by sympathy, took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.

entries.title: Luke 14:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Viz. Their thoughts, which were naked and open, naked (for the out-side) and dissected, quartered, and as it were cleft through the back-bone (for the in-side) before him with whom they had to deal, Heb. 4. 13.

entries.title: Luke 14:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Good must be done, however it be taken.

entries.title: Luke 14:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Jew of Tewkesbury, that would not be pulled out of the jakes whereinto he fell on their sabbath-day, perished deservedly.

entries.title: Luke 14:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yet ran away with the bit in their mouths.

entries.title: Luke 14:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ministers, though they may not be time-servers, yet they must be time-observers; and sharply reprove what they meet with amisse [ilegible] their people.

entries.title: Luke 14:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: When should a man rather feast then at the recovery of his lost rib?

entries.title: Luke 14:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As passing for a proud foole: a stile good enough for a self-exalter.

entries.title: Luke 14:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Honor est in honorante, therefore to be the lesse esteemed, because without us, and mostly but a puffe of stinking breath, not once to be valued.

entries.title: Luke 14:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matthew 23. 12.

entries.title: Luke 14:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Laudent [ilegible] esurientium viscera, non ructantium opulenta convivia, saith Jerom. Bishop (Hieron. ad [ilegible].) Hooper had his board of beggars, who were dayly served by four at a messe, with whole and wholesome meates, before himself sate (Act. & Mon.) down to dinner.

entries.title: Luke 14:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ preferres charity before curtesie.

entries.title: Luke 14:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Called theirs, because they only shall have joy of that day. It were well for the wicked if they might never rise to judgement, or trot directly to hell, and not be brought before the Lamb to be sentenced.

entries.title: Luke 14:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This man seems to have tasted (Heb. 6. 5.) of the good word of God, and of the powers of the world to come. Happy he, if he fed heartily thereon. This, saith Luther, is Sancta crapula.

entries.title: Luke 14:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: [ilegible] They are happy that get to heaven: they rest from their labours. The Ancients dined frugally, supped liberally. Be of good (Act. & Mon.) chear said that Martyr to her husband that suffered with her: for though wee have but an ill dinner, wee shall sup with Christ.

entries.title: Luke 14:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Licitis perimus omnes. More die by meat, then by poyson. Cavete, latet anguis in herba. What more lawfull then a farm? what more honorable, of all pleasures, (Vxori [ilegible] nolo mea. Martial.) then marriage? But these men had not so much bought their farms, &c. as were sold to them: not so much married wives, as were married to them.

entries.title: Luke 14:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This answers those that plead their necessities, and that they seek not [ilegible], (as farm upon farm, &c.) but only a sufficiency. What could be more necessary then Oxen, sith without them he could not follow his husbandry? Worldlinesse is a great hinderance to heaven, though a man cannot be charged with any great covetousnesse. These all excused themselves out of heaven, by bringing apologies why they could not go to heaven. Never yet any came to hell, but had some pretence for their coming thither. Our vile hearts will perswade us that there is some sense in sinning, and some reason to be mad.

entries.title: Luke 14:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Note that the voluptuary is peremtory, and saith flatly he cannot come. Sensuall hearts are void of the Spirit, Jude 18. 19. Miry places could not be healed by the Sanctuary waters, Ezek. 47. 11. fleshly lusts fight against the soul, 1 Pet. 2. 11. Those that dance to the timbrell and harp, say, Depart from us. Job 21. 11. Better be preserved in brine, then rot in hony.

entries.title: Luke 14:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And good reason he had: for Non modò plur is putare quod utile videatur, (Cit. [ilegible]. de [ilegible].) quam quod honestum, sed haec etiam inter se comparare, & in [ilegible], [ilegible] est, saith the honest heathen. Surely as Pharaoh said of the Israelites, They are intangled in the land, the wildernesse hath [ilegible] them in, Exod. 14. 3. so may we say of many, They are intangled in the creature, the world hath shut them in, they cannot come to Christ: They are shut up in a [ilegible], as those five Kings, Joshua 10. and have hardnesse of heart, as a great stone, rolled to the mouth, and honours, riches and pleasures as so many keepers, &c.

entries.title: Luke 14:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Much more his farm ([ilegible] ex odio reprobavit, respuit.) and his oxen. It was not these, but the inordinate love of these, that detained them, as Christ here intimateth. Your house, home, and goods, yea [ilegible], and all that ever ye have (saith that Martyr) (Master Brad.) God hath given you as love-tokens, to admonish you of his love, to (Acts and Mon. fol. 1492.) win your love to him again. Now will he try your love, whether ye set more by him, or by his tokens, &c.

entries.title: Luke 14:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Rodulphus Gualther being in Oxford, and beholding Christ-Church-Colledge said, Egregium opus: Cardinalis iste instituit collegium, & absolvit popinam. A pretty businesse! A Colledge begun, and a kitchin finished.

Counteth the cost] Let him that intendeth to build the tower of godlinesse, sit down first and cast up the cost, left, &c.

entries.title: Luke 14:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To consult, and so with good advice to make War. Romani sedendo vincunt, saith Varro. Thou shalt succour us out of the City, 2 Sam. 18. 3.

entries.title: Luke 14:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Mittamus preces & lachrymas cordis legatos, saith Cyprian. Currat poenitentia, ne [ilegible] sententia, saith Chrysologus. Repent, ere it be too late.

entries.title: Luke 14:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. That bids not farwell ([ilegible].) to all.

entries.title: Luke 14:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This was a sentence much in our Saviours mouth, Matt. 5. 13. Mark 9. 50. And is here used, to set forth the desperate condition of Apostates.

entries.title: Luke 15:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: CHrist familiarized himself with these despised persons, and thereby much wonne upon them. [ilegible] easily allureth, austerity discourageth; as it did that honest citizen, which having in himself a certain conflict of conscience, came to Master Hooper the Martyrs door for counsell. But being abashed at his austere (Act. & Mon. fol. 1366.) behaviour, durst not come in, but departed, seeking remedy of his troubled mind at other mens hands, &c.

entries.title: Luke 15:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Being sick of the devils disease, and doing his lusts, Joh. 8. 44

entries.title: Luke 15:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Would we then put harps into the Angels hands, ditties into their mouths? Repent.

entries.title: Luke 15:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
One Testor. Drachma enim valebat septem denarios cum dimidio. Breerwood de numb. Jud. c. 1. See the margent of our new Translation.

And sweep the house] Everrit, not Evertit, as the vulgar ([ilegible]) hath it corruptly: and Gregory with others were deceived by it in their discants and glosses, nothing to the purpose.

entries.title: Luke 15:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. His life. Our ([ilegible].) [ilegible] fe is called the life of our hands, Isaiah 57. 10. because it is upheld by the labour of our hands.

entries.title: Luke 15:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Convasatis veluti omnibus.

With riotous living] [ilegible], Not caring to save any part, [ilegible] ([ilegible], unsaveable.) nihil reservans, imò seipsum non servans, being such as safety it self could not save: whence the Latines call such a man Perditum, an undone person. Such were those of whom Seneca saith, that singulis auribus bina aut terna dependent patrimonia, hanged two or three good Lordships at their eares.

With riotous living] And such are those amongst us that turn lands into laces, great (H. S. millies in [ilegible] congessit. [ilegible].) rents into great ruffes, &c. The expences of Apicius his kitchin amounted to more then two millions of gold. He having eaten up his estate, and finding by his account that he had no more then 200000. crowns remaining, thought himself poor, and that this sufficed not to maintain his luxury: whereupon he drank down a glasse of poyson.

entries.title: Luke 15:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The stomack of man is a monster (saith one) which, being contained in so little a bulk as his body, is able to consume and devoure all things.

entries.title: Luke 15:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For till then he had been besides himself, and not his own worthy. Nebulo (saith one) cometh of Nabal; foole of [ilegible]: [ilegible] & [ilegible] are of neer affinity. Evill is Hebrew for a foole, &c. Wickednesse is called the foolishnesse of madnesse, Eccles. 7. 25.

entries.title: Luke 15:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, I have not only thee, but the whole heaven for a swift witnesse against me of mine offences and out-bursts. The heaven doth declare mine iniquity, and the earth riseth up against me; Job 20. 27.

entries.title: Luke 15:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Tantum velis & [ilegible] tihi praeoccurret, saith a Father. The Prodigall was but conceiving a purpose to return, and God met him, Isaiah 65. 24.

And kissed him] One would have thought he should have kicked him, or have killed him rather: but God is Pater miserationum, he is all bowels. The prodigall came, the father ran: God is slow to anger, swift to shew mercy.

entries.title: Luke 15:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Confesse, and the mends is made. Homo agnoscit, Deus ignoscit. Acknowledge but the debt, and he will crosse the book.

And am no more worthy, &c.] Infernus sum domine, said that ([ilegible], Hooper at his death, Act. & Mon. 1374.) holy Martyr; Lord, I am hell, but thou art heaven: I am soile, and a sink of sin, but thou a g acious God, &c.

entries.title: Luke 15:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ is that (Act. and Mon. fol. [ilegible].) fatted calfe, saith Mr. Tindall Martyr, slain to make penitent sinners good chear withall: and his right eousnesse is the goodly [ilegible] to cover the naked deformities of their sinnes.

entries.title: Luke 15:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So fareth it with every faithfull Christian. He was dead, but now lives, and cannot be insensible or ignorant of such a change.

entries.title: Luke 15:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Much lesse a [ilegible]. Hypocrites hold God to be in their debt, and through discontent weigh not his favours, as being never without some aylement.

entries.title: Luke 15:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
He sayth not, This my brother; he would not once owne him, because in poverty.

Which hath devoured thy living] q d. which you were so hasty to give unto him before your death (which you need not have done) and now he hath made a faire hand of it.

entries.title: Luke 15:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of himself he left his [ilegible] yet is he called the lost son.

entries.title: Luke 16:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: MAsters had need look well 1. To the chusing of their servants. (Salomon saw Jeroboam that he was industrious, and therefore without any respect at all to his Religion, he made him [ilegible] over all the charge of the house of Joseph; but to his [ilegible] disadvantage. [ilegible]. King 11. 28. with chapt. 12. 3.) 2. To the using of them: Most men make no other use of their servants then they doe of their beasts: whiles they may have their bodyes to doe their service, they care not if their soules serve the Devill. Hence they so [ilegible] prove false and [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 16:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: [ilegible] cum [ilegible] putet, said Cato. Stewards should often account with their masters.

entries.title: Luke 16:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They that will get wisedome, must both dig and beg. Prov. 2. 3. 4.

entries.title: Luke 16:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The scope of this parable is, ut [ilegible] charitate erga pauperes compensemus, saith Beza, that we expiate, as it were our prodigality by shewing mercy to the poore Dan, 4. 27.

entries.title: Luke 16:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Gr. that Lord, viz. the ([ilegible].) Steward Lord, not the Lord Christ who relateth this [ilegible]. [ilegible] if we understand it of Christ (as the Syriack here doth) yet He herein no more approveth of this Stewards false-dealing, then he doth of the Vsurers trade [ilegible]. 5. 27. or the theeves 1 Thess. 5. 2. Or the dancers Matth. 11. 17. or the Olympick games 1 Cor. 9. 24.

Because he had done wisely] The worldlings wisedome serves him (as the Ostriches wings) to make him out-run others upon earth, and in earthly things; but helps him never a whit toward heaven.

Are in their generation wiser] A swine that wanders can make better shift to get home to the trough, then a sheepe can to the fold. We have not received the spirit of this world 1 Cor. 2. 12. we cannot shift and plot as they can: but we have received a better thing. The fox is wise in his generation, the serpent subtile, so is the Devill too. When he was but young, he out-witted our [ilegible] parents, 2 Cor. 11. 3.

Then the children of light] As the Angels are called Angels of ([ilegible]. Adam.) light 2 Cor. 11. 14. Gods children are the onely earthly Angels, have a Goshen in their bosomes, can lay their hands on their hearts with dying Oecolampadius, and say, Hic sat lucis.

entries.title: Luke 16:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
quibus officia [ilegible] ([ilegible].) [ilegible] apud [ilegible], [ilegible], & [ilegible] is [ilegible]. Testifie your faith by your workes that God of his free-grace may commend and [ilegible] you.

Of the Mammon of [ilegible]] The next odious name to the Devill himselfe. This Mammon of iniquity, This wages of wickednesse is not gain, but losse.

They may receive you] That is, that [ilegible] the Angels, or [ilegible] riches, or the poore may let you into heaven.

entries.title: Luke 16:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: or, the uncertaine, [ilegible], deceitfull wealth of this world, which yet most rich men trust in, as if simply the better or safer for their abundauce. Hence [ilegible] derives Mammon from [ilegible], which signifieth to [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 16:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Riches are not properly ours, but Gods who hath entrusted us, and who doth usually agssine them to the wicked, those men of his hand, for their portion Psal. 17. 14. for all the heaven that they are ever to look for. Better things abide the Saints, who are here but forreiners, and must doe as they may.

Who shall give you that which is your owne] Quod nec eripi nec (Arist. [ilegible]. lib.) (2. cap. 23.) [ilegible] potest. Aristotle relateth a law like this made by [ilegible], That he that used not another mans horse well, should [ilegible] owne. ([ilegible] Naso [ilegible].)

entries.title: Luke 16:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. They blew their noses at him in scorne and derision. They fleared and jeared when they (Horat.) should have feared, and fled from the wrath to come.

entries.title: Luke 16:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A thing that I see in the night may shine, and that shining proceed from nothing but rottennesse. There may be malum [ilegible] in bona [ilegible], as in [ilegible] Zeale. Two things make a good Christian, good actions and good aymes. And though a good ayme doth not make a bad action good (as in Vzzah) yet a bad ayme makes a good action bad (Hos. 1. 4.) (as in [ilegible], whose justice was approved, but his pollicy punished.)

entries.title: Luke 16:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Not once named, as [ilegible] was, though never so little esteemed of men. God knew him by name as he did Moses: when the rich mans name is written in the earth, rottes above-ground, is left for a reproach. ([ilegible] Verbum est [ilegible]. Pasor.)

Which was clothed in purple, &c.] Gr. was commonly so cloathed. It was his every-dayes weare, as the word implyeth.

entries.title: Luke 16:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or Eleazar (as Tertullian and Prudentius call him) who having beene Abrahams faithfull servant, now resteth in his bosome.

entries.title: Luke 16:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Many poore folk have but prisoners pittances, which will neither keepe them alive, nor suffer them to dye.

The dogs came and licked his sores] When Sabinus was put to death for whifpering against Seianus, his dog lay down by his dead body, brought to his mouth the bread that was cast to him: And [ilegible] Sabinus was thrown into the river Tiber, the dog [ilegible] ([ilegible].) after him, to keepe him up, that he might not sinke into the bottome.

entries.title: Luke 16:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
A Metaphor from feasts say some: from fathers, say Others, who imbosome and hug their children when wearied with long running-about, or [ilegible] met with a knock, and come crying unto them.

And was carried by the Angels] Thorough the ayre, the Devils region, doe the Angels conduct the Saints at death: who may therefore call death as Jacob did the place where he met the Angels, (Act. & Mon. fol. 1907.) Mahanaim, Genes. 32. 2. For like as the [ilegible]-man was let down with his bed thorough the tiling before Jesus, Luke 5. 18. so is every good soule taken up in an heavenly couch thorough the roofe of his house, and carried into Christs presence by these heavenly Courtiers.

And was [ilegible]] Possibly with as much noysome stench and hurry in the ayre, as at Cardinall Wolseyes buriall. A terrible example there is in the book of Martyrs, of one Christopher [ilegible] an unmercifull Courtier, who suffering a poore Lazar to dye in a [ilegible] by him, did afterwards perish himselfe in a ditch.

entries.title: Luke 16:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Having punishment without pity, misery without mercy, sorrow without succour, crying without compassion, mischeife without measure, torments without end, and past imagination.

entries.title: Luke 16:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In his tongue he was most tortured, quia plus lingua peccaverat, saith Cyprian. So Nestorius ([ilegible] exesa. Evagr. l. 1.) the heretick had his tongue eaten up with worms. So Thomas Arundell Arch-bishop of Canterbury, and Steven Gardiner Bishop of Winchester, (two notorious persecutors) dyed with their (Acts & Mon. fol. 1622.) tongues thrust out big-swollen, and black with inflammation of their bodyes. A spectacle worthy to be noted of all such bloudy burning persecutors.

entries.title: Luke 16:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Sonne he calls him with respect either ad procreationem carnis, aut adaetatem, saith Piscator. But as it was but cold comfort to Dives in flames, that Abraham called him sonne; so those that have no more to shrowd themselves under, then a generall profession, shall find that an empty title yeelds but an empty comfort at last.

Receivedst thy good things] Wicked men then have not only a [ilegible] title, but a right before God to earthly things. It is their portion. Psal. 17. 14. And what Ananias had was his owne Act. 5. whiles he had it. God gave Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar for his paines at Tyre. It is hard to say, they are usurpers. They shall not (saith One) be called to an account at last day for possessing what they had, but for abusing that possession. As when the King gives a Traytour his life, he gives him meat and drink that may maintaine his life. So here God deales, not as that cr uell D' [ilegible] did who starved some prisoners after he had given them quarter, (Grimst. Hist. of Netherl.) saying, Though I promised you your lives, I promised not to find you meat.

entries.title: Luke 16:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: viz. by the unmoveable ([ilegible].) and immutable decree of God, called mountaines of brasse ([ilegible]. [ilegible].) Zech. 6. 1. from betweene which all effects and actions come forth as so many charets.

entries.title: Luke 16:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This he wisheth, not for their good, but for his owne. For he knew that if they were damned, he should be double damned, because they were brought thither partly by his lewd and loose example.

entries.title: Luke 16:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hell is to be escaped by hearing the word read and preached. Joh. 5. 25. Esay 55. 3.

entries.title: Luke 16:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As Lazarus did, and yet they listened as little to him as to Christ. Joh. 12. but sought to kill him also.

entries.title: Luke 17:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A Most necessary request in this case. For the more any man beleeveth that God for Christs sake hath pardoned him, the readier he will be to pardon others.

entries.title: Luke 17:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It implies 1 readinesse: 2 nimblenesse, handinesse, and handsomenesse. A loose [ilegible] and [ilegible] mind is unfit to serve God. The Deacons cried of old in the Church-meetings Oremus, [ilegible], Let us pray, let us attend to prayer, &c.

entries.title: Luke 17:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or, our debt: and ([ilegible] [ilegible] the Church. [ilegible]. [ilegible] [ilegible].) it is no matter of merit to pay debts. This made [ilegible] founder of New-Colledge, &c. professe, he trusted in Jesus Christ alone for Salvation. Charles the Fifth did the like, when he came to die. And in times of Popery, the ordinary instruction appointed to be given to men upon their death beds, was, that they should look to come to glory, not by their own merits, but by the vertue and merit of Christs passion: that they should place their whole ([ilegible]. [ilegible] in a Serm. [ilegible] Eph. 4. 13.) confidence in his death only, and in no other thing: and that they should interpose his death betwixt God and their sins, betwixt them and Gods anger.

entries.title: Luke 17:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: These sought themselves only in their prayers as do hypocrites: and nought esteemed the love of Christ. So did those that fasted to themselves, (Cant. 51.) [ilegible]. 7. more to get off their chains then their sins. Ephrain is an empty vine, he [ilegible] fruit to himself. The Church keeps her fruit for her beloved.

entries.title: Luke 17:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As if yee were already cleansed. They did so, though they saw no sense for it: and before they came to the Priest, they were cleansed indeed. Make your requests known to God with thanksgiving, Philip. 4. 6. As who should say, make account to speed, and be ready with your thanks, as if you had what you ask of God.

entries.title: Luke 17:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Its ten to one if any return to give thanks. Men make prayer their refuge, but not their recompence. [ilegible] returned not according to his receipts.

And with a loud [ilegible]] He was as earnest in praises, as he had been in prayers. Our thanks should be larger and louder then our requests; because God prevents us with many mercies, and denies nothing: we have it either in mony or monies worth.

entries.title: Luke 17:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A thankfull man is worth his ([ilegible]. [ilegible]. Barn. de Consid. lib 4.) weight in gold. Sed perrarò grati homines reperiuntur, saith the Oratour. Plerique ut accipiant. importuni, donec acceperint, inquieti; ubi acceperint, ingrati, saith the Father. Most pray, but pay not: they make prayer their refuge, but not their recompence.

entries.title: Luke 17:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ keeps count how many favours men receive from him, and will call them to a particular account thereof. He is an austere man this way.

entries.title: Luke 17:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Syriack, and some others [ilegible] these words question-wise, and so it is more emphaticall: Are there not found that returned? &c. q. d. That's admirable, that's abhominable.

entries.title: Luke 17:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This they asked in [ilegible]. q. d. You tell us oft of the kingdom of God, and that it is at hand: but when comes it once? All things continue as they did, &c.

Cometh not with observation] That is, with outward pomp, or superstitious seeking after.

entries.title: Luke 17:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It is spiritual, Rom. 14. 17. Or, it is among you, but that you cannot see wood for trees. You seek me as absent, whom you reject present.

entries.title: Luke 17:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. This doctrine concerns you also, as well as the perverse Pharisees. You shall be ere long at a great losse for me: look to it therefore and bestirre you.

entries.title: Luke 17:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. From mine Ascention, and so forwards, you are not to look for me again till I come to judgement: and then I come on a sudden. Many devices there are in the minds of some, to think that Jesus Christ shall come from heaven again, and reign here upon earth a Thousand years. But (Mr. Cotton upon the 7 Vials.) they are (saith a good Divine) but the mistakes of some high expressions in Scripture, which describe the judgements powred out upon Gods enemies, in making a way to the Jewes conversion, by the pattern of the last judgement.

entries.title: Luke 17:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An elegant Asyndeton. For the reason whereof, see the Note on Matt. 24. 38.

entries.title: Luke 17:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It is not said here as vers. 27. they married wives: they affected rather those odious [ilegible], ([ilegible].) qui non utrinque resolvunt. The Turkish Bashaes have their [ilegible], which, are their serious loves: for their wives are used (Blounts Voyage, pag. 14.) but to dresse their meat, to laundresse, and for reputation, saith one that had been amongst them. Sodomy (saith he) in the Levant is not held a vice.

entries.title: Luke 17:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A fair Sun-shine-morning had a foul dismall evening. Neseis quid serus [ilegible] vehat. Thou (Horat.) knowest not what a great-bellyed day may bring forth, [ilegible] crede diem tibi diluxisse supremum. Think every day the last day.

entries.title: Luke 17:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Security ushereth in destruction. The Judge standeth before the door, as is easie to foresee: (Jam. 5.) Watch therefore.

entries.title: Luke 17:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An hyperbolicall expression, usuall among the Jewes, to denote matter of haste.

entries.title: Luke 17:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who either out of curiosity (Vt [ilegible] ab uncto [ilegible].) or covetousnesse turnd her but, and she was turned. We are as hardly drawn off the world, as a Dog from a fat morsell. Those that set forth of Italy with Galeacius Marquesse of Vicum (who left all for the liberty of conscience at Geneva) many of them when they came to the borders of Italy, and considering what ([ilegible] of [ilegible]. by Mr. [ilegible].) they forsook, first looked back, afterward went back again, and were taken by the Spanish Inquisition, and made publikly to abjure the Christian religion. Remember the horrible history of [ilegible] of old, and the lamentable case of Spira alate, said the Lady (Acts & Mon. sol 1291.) Jane Gray prisoner, to Harding the Apostate. Lege historiam, (saith one) ne fias historia: lege judicia, ne fias exemplum [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 17:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or, Whither Lord, viz. shall they be taken, of whom thou speakest? To heaven, saith he. See the Note on Matt. 24. 28.

entries.title: Luke 18:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: GRaece, Not shrink back, as Sluggards in work, or Cowards ([ilegible].) in Warre. Prayer should be redoubled and reinforced, as those Arrowes of deliverance, 2. Kings 13. 19. The woman of Canaan prayes on when denyed: And Jacob holds with his hands, when his thigh is lamed. He wrestled with slight and might, ([ilegible] post nau fragium tentantur [ilegible].) he raised dust, as the word signifies, and would not away without a blessing. James surnamed the Just, (Christs Kinsman) had his knees made as hard as Camels knees with much praying, as [ilegible] ([ilegible]. Epist. 81.) [ilegible]. Father Latimer during his imprisonment, was (Act. & Mon. sol. 1579.) [ilegible] constant and instant in prayer, that oftt-[ilegible] he was not able to [ilegible] off his knees, without help. Yea Paulus Emilius, being to ([ilegible].) fight with Perses King of Macedony, would not give over [ilegible] to his God Hercules, till he saw certain arguments of a victory. As loathing of meat (saith a Divine) and painfulnesse of speaking are two symptomes of a sick body: so irksomnesse of [ilegible], and carelesnesse of hearing, of a sick soule.

entries.title: Luke 18:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: These two, [ilegible] of God and shame of the world, God hath given to men as [ilegible] to restraine them from outrage. But sinne hath oaded such [ilegible] impudency in some mens faces, that they dare do any thing.

entries.title: Luke 18:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A downright request, without either Logick or Rhetorick to set it forth, or inforce it: to each us that though our prayers be but blunt or broken language if importunate, they shall prevaile neverthelesse.

entries.title: Luke 18:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: There is a passive injustice. Non [ilegible] nocens, sed [ilegible] fuit, saith Ausonius of Claudius. Not to do justice is injustice.

entries.title: Luke 18:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. She buffet me, or club me down. ([ilegible].) God must be pressed in prayer, till we put him (as you would say) (Obtundat.) (Vota fundimus [ilegible] tundimus Deum tangimus misericordiam [ilegible].) to the blush, or leave a blot in his face, unlesse we may be masters of our requests.

entries.title: Luke 18:6-7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hic paria non inter se conferuntur, sed minus cum majore, saith Beza.

entries.title: Luke 18:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: When they are at the (Tertul. Apol.) [ilegible] most under. When their enemies are above feare, and they below hope; when there is not faith in Earth to beleeve, then are there bowels in Heaven to releive and restore them.

entries.title: Luke 18:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: God oft staies so long, till the Saints have done looking for him, when they have forgot their prayers; &c. he comes, as it were out of an engine.

entries.title: Luke 18:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Pray to be preserved from this perillous pinacle of self exaltation.

entries.title: Luke 18:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A Doeg may set his foot as far and further within the Sanctuary, as a David. The Pharisee and Publican went both of them up to private prayer.

entries.title: Luke 18:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Non vulnera sed muner a [ilegible], ([ilegible]. Basil.) he shewes not his want but his worth: and stands not only upon his comparisons, but upon his disparisons, I am not as this Publican. No, for thou art worse: yea for this, because thou thinkest ([ilegible].) thee better. But of Pharisees it might be said as Arnobius did of the Gentiles, Apud vos optimi censentur, quos [ilegible] pessimorum ([ilegible].) [ilegible] facit. They are very good that are not very bad.

[ilegible]] Pride wears a triple crown with this motio, Tra. [ilegible], Non obedio, [ilegible]. This Pharisee held himself [ilegible], and all others a [ilegible] only, as Basil of [ilegible] hath it: He takes his poor counter and sets it down for a Thousand pounds; he prizeth himself above the market.

entries.title: Luke 18:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Cardinall Bellarmine did more: for he fasted thrice a week, saith he that writes his life. John ArchBishop ([ilegible]. D. [ilegible].) of [ilegible], he who first affected the stile of Universall Bishop, was sirnamed Nesteutes, from his frequent fasting. Munday and Thursday were the Pharisees fasting-dayes: because Moses went up to the Mount on a Thursday, and came down on a Munday, saith [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 18:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
In token of indignation, and that he would have smitten his sin so hard, if he could have come at it.

God be mercifull, &c.] Here was much in few. The Publican [ilegible] much: though he spake little. As a body without a soul, much wood without fire, a bullet in a gun without powder, so are words in prayer without spirit. Oratio brevis penetrat caelum. The hottest springs send forth their waters by ebullitions.

entries.title: Luke 18:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Pharisee was not at all justified: Neither is there More or Lesse in justification. But our Saviour here useth a popular kind of expression.

entries.title: Luke 18:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Saint Mark saith that this (Mark 10. [ilegible] [ilegible].) Ruler came running, which argues his earnestnesse; and in a man of quality was [ilegible]: for such walk softly for most part, and in state.

entries.title: Luke 18:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yea all things. But our Saviour speaketh thus by an holy irony.

entries.title: Luke 18:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Caveant ergi divites (saith an Interpreter) & solicitè; mane, vesperi, interdiù, noctu, secum de periculosa vitae suae, atione commententur. Let rich men therefore weigh their danger, and beware.

entries.title: Luke 18:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Prejudicate opinions of Christs earthly kingdom hung as so many bullets at their eye lids, that they could not perceive so plain a truth.

entries.title: Luke 19:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
CHrist is that good Shepheard, that knoweth all his sheep, and calleth them by name.

Make haste and come downe] Heaven is a matter of greatest [ilegible]: We must not adjourne as he did once, In [ilegible] seria, more weighty [ilegible] till to morrow.

To day I must abide at thy house] Christ not only invites, but even obtrudes himself, as it [ilegible], upon [ilegible]: Its happy having [ilegible] guests. He doth the same to us, when he sends unto us his poor servants to presse upon our charity. Unworthy we are surely to give an almes to poor Christ, &c.

entries.title: Luke 19:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
See the like in Tyrus converted, [ilegible]. 23. 17, 18 [ilegible]

I restore him four fold] Which was the law for things stollen. Fraud is no better then theft. Restitution [ilegible] necessary to [ilegible] of [ilegible]. God hates [ilegible] ex rapina, as Sultan [ilegible] could tell his Councellour Pyrrhus, who perswaded him to bestow ([ilegible]. Hist. sol. 567.) [ilegible] great wealth he [ilegible] taken from the Persian Merchants, upon some notable Hospitall for releif of the poor: The dying Turk commanded it rather to be restored to the right owners, which was done accordingly; to the great shame of many Christians, who mind nothing [ilegible] then restitution, &c. When Henry the Third of England had sent the Frier Minors a load of [ilegible] to [ilegible] them, they returned the same with this message; [ilegible] he ought not to give almes of what he had rent from the poor, neither (Daniels hist. of Engl. 109.) would they accept of that abhominable gift. Master [ilegible] saith, If ye make no [ilegible] of goods [ilegible], ye shall cough in [ilegible]. [ilegible]

entries.title: Luke 19:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, freely elected, Romans. 9. 1. a. [ilegible] of [ilegible] faith, Rom. 4. 12. and a doer of his works, Job. 8. 39. Who then can say but he is his son, and shall rest in his bosome?

entries.title: Luke 19:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: [ilegible] [of sending a lamb to this [ilegible] of the earth, [ilegible]. [ilegible] with the [ilegible] of their lips, [ilegible]. 14. 3. Such [ilegible] are [ilegible] where; such dust-heapes are found in every corner.

entries.title: Luke 19:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He went, at his Ascention; and returns at the generall Resurrection: At what time he will first reckon with his servants, and then with his enemies. Judgement shall then also begin at Gods own house.

entries.title: Luke 19:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not my paines, but thy pound hath done it. By the grace of God I am that I am, saith Paul that constantissimus gratiae Praedicator, as Austin calleth him.

entries.title: Luke 19:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Unto the table, or (according ([ilegible].) to some coppies) unto the Usurers, whom Beza here rightly calleth humani certè gener is perniciosissimas pestes, the most pernicious pests of mankind.

entries.title: Luke 19:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Howbeit the Beast and the false Prophet, that is, the Pope and his Janizaries, shal not have the favour to be flain as the common sort of Christs enemies are, but shall be cast alive into the burning lake, tormented more exquisitly, Revelations 19. 20, 21.

entries.title: Luke 19:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To meet death in the face: this was true magnanimity. Herein he shewed himself the captain of our salvation, though perfected by sufferings.

entries.title: Luke 19:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bethphage was one mile out of Jerusalem, Bethany two.

entries.title: Luke 19:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Into Bethphage, that was in their veiw as they went from Bethany.

entries.title: Luke 19:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
That common slaughter-house of the Prophets. Our Lord is said to have been slain at Rome, Revelations 11. 8. because crucified at Jerusalem by the Roman authority.

And wept over it] Shall not we weep over the ruines of so many fair and flourishing Churches, that now lie in the dirt? Christ wept in this day of his solemne Inauguration. It shall be in our last triumph only that all teares shall be wiped from our eyes; till then our passions must be mixed, according to the occasions.

entries.title: Luke 19:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
They had cognitionem historicam non mysticam, speculativam non affectivam, apprehensionis, non approbationis, discursivam, non experimentalem.

At least in this thy day] The time of grace is fitly called a Day in regard of 1 Revelation. 2 Adornation. 3 Consolation. 4 Distinction. 5 Speedy preterition. Amend before the draw-bridge be taken up. No man can say, he shall have 12 hours to his day.

But now they are hid from thine eyes:] Yet they lived under the Ministry long after, and no outward change to be discerned. As Plutarch writes of Hannibal, that when he could have taken Rome, he would not; when he would, he could not; so the Procrastinators.

entries.title: Luke 19:43
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
God hath his dayes for vengeance, as man hath his day for repentance. There is a Prime of every mans life, and of every mans. Ministry. The Levite lingered so long, that he lost his Concubine; she came short home: so doth many a mans soul for like reason.

Shall cast a trench about thee] Because like the wild-asse, thou wouldst not otherwise be tamed, and kept within compasse of Gods Commandements. ([ilegible].)

entries.title: Luke 19:48
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Hanged on him, as the Bee doth on the flower, the babe on the breast, or the little bird on the bill of her Damme. Christ drew the people after him, as it were, by the golden chain of his heavenly eloquence.

entries.title: Luke 20:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: GRaece, Came suddenly upon him] As an expected storme: the ([ilegible].) Devill drove them.

entries.title: Luke 20:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. If John were sent by God to testifie, as he did, there is no colour of cause why ye should question mine authority?

entries.title: Luke 20:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gods servants should be ready with their answer upon sudden assaults, and not to seek of such arguments as may stop the mouth of an adversary. When a [ilegible] Jesuite asked, Where was your religion before Luther? Answer was presently returned, In the Bible, where your religion never was.

entries.title: Luke 20:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Viz. That they should ever kill the Sonne of God sent unto them. We cannot get men to beleive that their hearts are half so bad, or their wayes so dangerous, as the preacher makes of them.

entries.title: Luke 20:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. If it be not so as I say, that you shall kill the Messiah, how is it that the Scripture saith as much? presse men with Scripture-testimonies: that's the readiest way of sound conviction.
