It was a good speech of Augustine to [ilegible], contesting with him for audience: [ilegible] me, hear me, said the Heretique. Nay, saith Augustine, [ilegible] ego [ilegible], [ilegible] tu me, sed ambo [ilegible] Apostoium [ilegible], [ilegible] non cognovi, &c. It is not I say, or what thou saiest, but what the Scripture saith, that we [ilegible] stand to.

entries.title: Luke 20:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Fishers, that with net and bait catch the silly fish, and feed on them: such were these Emissaries, ([ilegible].) these catch-poles. (Aretius.)

entries.title: Luke 20:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hence some collect, that the difference of sexes [ilegible] continue after the resurrection: wherefore else should our Saviour say, that they shall then neither marry nor be given in marriage? Sed hic [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 20:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Even in their bodies also, which he now by [ilegible] refineth; and shall as certainly raise, as if they were already raised, sith all things are present with him.

entries.title: Luke 21:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: THat is, two eight parts of an half-penny, saith the Syriack. See the Notes on Mark 12. 41, 42, &c.

entries.title: Luke 21:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Whilest the valour of the Martyrs and the savagenesse of the Persecutors strove together, till both, exceeding nature and belief, bred wonder and [ilegible] in beholders and hearers.

entries.title: Luke 21:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, Enjoy yourselves, however the world goes with you. He that cannot have patience, had need make up his pack, and get out of the world: for here's (Camd. Elizab. fol. 495.) no being for him. Burleigh Lord Treasurer was wont to say, that he overcame envy more by patience then [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 21:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By Cestius [ilegible], a little before that fatall siege by [ilegible]. So God gave his people this sign, to take best course for their own safety.

entries.title: Luke 21:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Gentiles then shall not alwayes tread down Jerusalem. Those Kings of the East the Jewes may, likely, [ilegible] their way prepared to it, through [ilegible]. [ilegible]. 16. 12. and Jerusalem be again inhabited by them, (Zach. 12. 6.) even [ilegible] [ilegible]. But this will be not long [ilegible] day, [ilegible] 25.

entries.title: Luke 21:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: What marvell though [ilegible] men be dispirited, and even ring their bels backwards, when they shall see all on a light fire? Moses himself may tremble at the terrour of the mount, and Abraham shew some trepidation in such a fright.

entries.title: Luke 21:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Disciples [ilegible] had in them the common poyson of nature: and so, were obnoxious even to the most reproachfull evils. That [ilegible], if watered with the temptation of Satan, what sinne may it not produce in the best, unlesse God prevent?

entries.title: Luke 21:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Great is the Emphasis ([ilegible]) of this word (saith learned Beza) for it gives us to understand that we owe all to the free election of God, who loved us first, and so accepted us for worthy; Rev. 3. 4.

entries.title: Luke 22:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: IT is good to bring Bibles to Church. Socrates relates of one ([ilegible]. lib. 7. cap. 5.) Sabbatius a Novation Bishop, that reading this text, added such things of his own as carried away many simple people from the faith.

entries.title: Luke 22:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not put him to death as Judges, but kill him as cut-throates. So Act. ([ilegible].) 2. 23.

entries.title: Luke 22:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He stood but at the door till now, that the businesse was concluded on.

entries.title: Luke 22:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Suopte ingenio, [ilegible] reprobi Angeli, saith an Interpreter.

entries.title: Luke 22:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By mutuall stipulation (saith ([ilegible].) Beza) wherein the one asketh, Dost thou promise to do such a thing? the other answereth, I do promise. Like as of old it was, Credis? Credo. Abrenuncias? Abrenuncia. Beleevest thou? I do beleeve. Forsakest thou? I do forsake.

entries.title: Luke 22:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It must be our care to cast out all filthinesse of flesh and spirit (that old leaven) before we communicate, 1 Cor. 5. 7. First throw the baggage into the brook Kidron (the town-ditch) and then kill the Passeover, 2 Chron. 30. 14.

entries.title: Luke 22:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: How much more should we come with strong affections and lusty appetites to this holy Supper? It is a vertue here to be an holy glutton, and to drink hearty draughts; that we may go from the Table, as Christ from Jordan, full of the holy Ghost. For this end consider what is before thee, as Prov. 23. 1. not to restraine appetite, but to provoke it. And the rather because Christ thus earnestly thirsted after our salvation, though he knew it should cost him so dear. See Luke 12. 50.

entries.title: Luke 22:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Untill the old Passeover be abolished, and the New brought in place, by my death and resurrection.

entries.title: Luke 22:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The cup of the common supper, John 13. 2, 3.

entries.title: Luke 22:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Therefore the Lord had not perfectly pointed out the traytour to them: or if he did, they either heardnot, or heeded not.

entries.title: Luke 22:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This was so much the worse in them, because immediatly after the Sacrament, and before the Passion, which our Saviour had told them should fall out within two dayes after. Neither was this the first time that they had thus faulted, and were reproved for it.

entries.title: Luke 22:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
In striving for precedency the Disciples shew'd themselves but Gentiles, who stand upon their birth and priviledges.

Exercise Lordship over them] As he did with a witnesse (of (Joh. Manlii loc. com. 636) whom Melancthon writeth) that wrung mony from his miserable subjects, by knocking out their teeth, one by one, till he had what he would.

entries.title: Luke 22:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Agrippa having suffered imprisonment for wishing Caius Emperour, the first thing Caius did after he came to the Empire, was to preferre Agrippa to a Kingdome. He gave him also a chaine of gold as heavie as the chaine of iron that was upon him in prison. And shall not Christ richly reward all those his suffering servants?

entries.title: Luke 22:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. I bequeath as by my last Will ([ilegible], [ilegible].) and Testament. See Heb. 9. 17.

entries.title: Luke 22:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As Mephibosheth and Chinham at Davids table; which was an high favour.

entries.title: Luke 22:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
q. d. Mi charissime Simon. Piscat.

Satan hath desired, &c.] As a challenger desireth to have one of the other-side to combat with, as Goliah did. He cannot harm us without leave. So he desired to have Job, and had him.

That he may sift you] Cribratione Satanae non perditur, sed purgatur frumentum, saith Zanchy. See the Note on Matthew 3. 12.

entries.title: Luke 22:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
So the plaister is ready made before the wound be given: for else the patient might perish, as those do that are stung with scorpions, if not presently anointed with [ilegible] of scorpions.

That thy faith fail not] It is our faith that Satan chiefly assaulteth: (Seneca.) He knowes that nihil retinet qui fidem perdidit.

Strengthen thy brethren] So he doth notably, in both his Epistles, dooming Apostates most severely, 2. Pet. 2.

entries.title: Luke 22:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For privacy sake to pray, though [ilegible] to leave their company, thorough extreame perplexity; which made him return so oft to them, calling upon them to watch with him.

entries.title: Luke 22:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He was so astonied with the greatnesse of his present pressures, that he seems for a time to suffer some kind of forgetfulnesse of his office.

entries.title: Luke 22:44
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
[ilegible] saith a Greek Father. Alphonsus is honoured in Histories for this, that he abased himself so far, as to help one of his subjects out of a ditch. Shall not Christ much more be honoured that helped all his out of the ditch of damnation?

Great drops of bloud] Clotty bloud issuing through flesh and skin in great abundance. Oecolampadius tels of a certain poor man, ([ilegible],) who being kept hanging in the trusse of the cord (which is a certain hanging by the hands behind, having a weighty stone fastened at their feet) the space of six hours, the sweat that dropt from his (Act. and Mon. fol. 805.) body for very pain and anguish, was almost bloud. But here was no (almost) in our Saviours bloudy sweat; whiles, without any externall violence meerly by the force of his own saddest thoughts working upon him, sanguinem congelatum quasi extruserit. So great was Scanderbegs ardor in battell, that the bloud burst out of his (Bucholcer.) lips. But from our Champions not lips only, but whole body, burst out a bloudy sweat. Not his eyes only were fountains of tears, or his head waters, as Jeremy wished Chap. 9. 1. but his whole body was turned, as it were, into rivers of bloud: A sweet comfort to such as are cast down for that, that their sorrow for sin is not so deep and soaking, as they could desire.

entries.title: Luke 22:45
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who should have waked, (Socrates Theodoret.) and wiped off his sweat (as the Angell did Theodorus the Martyrs) but they rather added to it by their security.

entries.title: Luke 22:48
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Sic Judaei, sub praetextu ([ilegible].) pietatis maximè delinquebant; & Deo osculum sine amore [ilegible]. Julian the Apostate was no friend to Basil, though he wrote to him [ilegible]. Nor was Libanius the more to be beleived for saying [ilegible]. (In [ilegible] ad [ilegible].) If Basil commend me, I despise other mens worse censures.

entries.title: Luke 22:49
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But before he could answer, Peter smot: which might easily have cost him his life. Quod [ilegible], ne feceris, is a safe rule.

entries.title: Luke 22:51
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: After he had laid them flat on the ground. So he tryed them both wayes: but nothing would do.

entries.title: Luke 22:53
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The dark places of the (1 Cor. [ilegible].) earth are full of the habitations of cruelty, Psal. 74. 20. Creatures ([ilegible] Tim.) kept in the dark are [ilegible] and furious. Had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. I did it ignorantly, saith Paul concerning his persecuting the Saints.

entries.title: Luke 22:61
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A stroke from guilt broke Judas his heart into despair: but a look from Christ brak Peters heart into teares.

entries.title: Luke 23:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: GRaece, Turning them up-side down, wreathing them from ([ilegible]) their right minds. So Verse 5. He Stirreth up the [ilegible] ([ilegible].) Gr. He maketh an earthquake in them; rectam toll it de cardine [ilegible], he throws them off the hinges.

entries.title: Luke 23:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As if he had got some [ilegible] or inchanter, that would shew him some pleasant sight.

entries.title: Luke 23:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Princes use to [ilegible] the undecencies of Embassadours by denying them audience: as if [ilegible] were the way royall to revenge a wrong. Christ [ilegible] not a word to [ilegible] (saith one) because Herod had taken away his voice, by beheading the Baptist, who was vox clamantis.

entries.title: Luke 23:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. With great intention ([ilegible]) of spirit, and contention of speech. Clamant, ut Stent or a vincant.

entries.title: Luke 23:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Gr. Made no body of him. ([ilegible])

Arrayed him in a gorgeous robe] Or a whit robe, as the old Interpreter hath it. Pilates souldiers clad our Saviour in purple, ([ilegible]) (a colour more affected by the Romans) Herod in white, as more affected by the Jewish Nobility.

entries.title: Luke 23:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Two dogs that are fighting, can easily agree to pursue the Hare that passeth by them. Martiall brings in the Hare thus complaining; In me omnis terraeque aviumque, marisque rapina est: Forsitan & coeli, si canis astra tenet.

In littore Siculo cum lepus canum [ilegible] vim [ilegible], [ilegible] (Bodin. [ilegible]. Nat. 359.) [ilegible] marimo captus dicitur: Est enim voracissima [ilegible], saith Bodin. The wicked can easily unite against the Saints.

entries.title: Luke 23:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I read of one that did verily think that Pilate was an honest man, because he was so unwilling to crucifie Christ. But this arose only from the restraint of naturall conscience against so foul a fact.

entries.title: Luke 23:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Jewes before they were banished out of this Kingdome, threw bags of poyson into the Wells and Fountains that the people were to drink of; and so indeavovred to poyson them all: so deale those that sowe sedition, these are the Pests, the botches of humane society.

entries.title: Luke 23:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: We are not so much to lament dolorous sufferings (as Papists use to do in their histrionicall descriptions of his passion) as to lay to heart and lament our sinnes the cause of [ilegible] When a Papist came to Master Hooper at the stake (Act. & Mon. sol. 1373.) and said, Sir, I am sorry to see you thus. Be sorry for thy self man, (said hearty Hooper) and lament thine own wickednesse: for I [ilegible] well, I thank God, and death to me for Christs sake is welcome.

entries.title: Luke 23:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Better be so, then bring forth children to the murtherer. Hence Hoseas prayes for barrennesse as a blessing on his people, Hos. 9. 14.

entries.title: Luke 23:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Lo little sucklings also are here called dry trees, [ilegible]-wood, such as Gods wrath will soon kindle upon.

entries.title: Luke 23:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As sad a sight to our Saviour, as the bodies of his slain wife and children were to Mauricius the Emperour, who was soon after to be slain also by the command of the traytour Phocas. Let us learn to consider the tyranny and deformity of sin as oft as we passe thorough Church-yards, and Charnell-houses.

entries.title: Luke 23:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the sweet mercy of Christ mindfull and carefull of his enemies, when the paines of hell had taken hold of him, and they, like so many breathing devils, were tormenting him. Pendebat & tamen petebat, saith Augustine. He was slain by them, and yet he begged for them.

entries.title: Luke 23:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: [ilegible]. Blew their noses at him. ([ilegible])

entries.title: Luke 23:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In stead of wine, which Kings drink much off.

entries.title: Luke 23:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This venerable Elogy and Epitaph, set upon our Saviours Crosse, proclaimed him King of all religion, having reference to the Hebrews, of all wisdom, to the Greeks, of all power to the Latines.

entries.title: Luke 23:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Sic plectimur a Deo, nec flectimur tamen, (saith Salvian) corripimur, sed non corrigimur. There are many, quos multò facilius fregeris, quàm flexeris, saith ([ilegible].) Buchanan. Monoceros interimi potest, capi non potest. The wicked are the worse for that they suffer, and will sooner break then bend.

entries.title: Luke 23:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Silent he was for a while, and therefore seemed to consent; till, hearing Christs prayers and the enemies outrages, he brake out into this brave confession, worthy to be written in letters of gold.

entries.title: Luke 23:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By this penitent prayer he made his crosse a Jacobs ladder, whereby the Angels descended to fetch up his soul. So did Leonard Caesar burnt at Rappa in Bavaria, whose last words were these, Lord Jesu suffer with me, support ([ilegible]. [ilegible].) me, give me strength: I am thine, save me, &c. See the Note on Matt. 27. 38.

entries.title: Luke 23:43
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
See the infinite love of Christ to penitent sinners, in that when he hung upon the tree, and was paying dear [ilegible] mans sin, he rejected not this malefactors petition. Shall he not hear us now that all is paid and finished?

To day shalt thou be with me] This is not every mans happinesse. A pardon is sometimes given to one upon the gallows: but who so [ilegible] to that, the rope may be his hire. It is not good to put it upon the Psalm of Miserere, and the neck-verse (saith one:) for sometimes he proves no clark.

entries.title: Luke 23:47
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bennet the [ilegible] in King Henry the Eighths daies, being brought to execution, the most part of the people (he exhorted them with such (Acts & Mon. fol 949.) gravity and sobriety) as also the Scribe who wrote the sentence of (Ibid. 1156. & 1423.) condemnation against him, did pronounce and confesse that he was Gods servant, and a good man. So when Wiseheart and March, the Martyrs, went toward the stake, they were justified by the beholders, as innocent and godly persons.

entries.title: Luke 23:51
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This proved him to be a good man and a just, as Psal. 1. 1. Sir John Cheek was drawn in for fear of death to be present at the condemnation of some of the (Acts & Mon. 1774.) Martyrs. The remorse whereof so mightily wrought upon his heart, that not long after he left this mortall life: whose fall, though it was full of infirmity, yet his rising again by repentance was great, and his end comfortable, saith Master Fox.

Waited for the kingdom of God] Gr. Entertained and embraced ([ilegible]) it.

entries.title: Luke 24:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ABout which time (probably) our Saviour rose.

entries.title: Luke 24:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Per os mulieris mors ante processerat, per os mulieris vita reparatur, saith Ambrose. So Chap. 1. an Angel of light communeth with a woman about mans salvation, as an Angel of darknesse had done, Gen. 3. about his fall and destruction.

entries.title: Luke 24:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Set on with great earnestnesse. ([ilegible] a [ilegible] particula [ilegible] & [ilegible] valde dico.)

entries.title: Luke 24:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Obstipo capite & propenso collo. We need not doubt therefore of the certainty of this history of Christs resurrection.

entries.title: Luke 24:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: About sixe miles.

entries.title: Luke 24:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So did Elias and Elisha, when the heavenly chariot came to sunder them. Christ is still with two or three met for such an holy purpose.

entries.title: Luke 24:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ut ulcus suum discipuli detegerent, [ilegible] susciperent, saith Theophylact. That they may tell their own disease, and receive healing.

entries.title: Luke 24:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Gr. That ye tosse one ([ilegible] ut cum [ilegible].) to another, as a ball is tossed betwixt two or more.

And are sad] Christ loves not to see his Saints sad: hee questions them as Joseph did his prisoners, Wherefore look ye so sadly to day, Gen. 40. 7? and as the king did Nehemiah, Chap. 3. 2.

entries.title: Luke 24:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
They that hold the other of these two to have been Saint Luke, are [ilegible] by the preface he hath set before the Acts, saith Beza.

Art thou only a stranger, &c.] Tragedies have no prologues, (Natat. Comes.) as comedies have: because it is supposed, that all men take knowledge of publike calamities.

entries.title: Luke 24:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yea and more then a Prophet. But the disciples were wondrous ignorant, till the spirit came down upon them, Act. 2.

entries.title: Luke 24:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. Indeed nowwe cannot tell what to say to it. Here their hope hangs the wing extreamly, their ([ilegible]. Epicter.) buckler is much battered, and needs beating out again. Ferendum & sperandum, said the Philosopher. And good men find it more easie to bear evill, then to wait for good, Hebrews 10. 36.

entries.title: Luke 24:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Those in a Lethargy must have double the quantity of physick that others have. Some (Tit. 1. 12. 13.) slow-bellies must be sharply rebuked, that they may be sound in the faith.

entries.title: Luke 24:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ne Jesum quidem audias gloriosum, nisi videris crucifixum, saith Luther in an Epistle to Melancthon. ([ilegible] [ilegible].) Agentem fortiter [ilegible] aliquid pati, said a Theban souldier, out of Pindarus, to Alexander, when he had received a wound in battle: For the which sentence, he liberally rewarded him.

entries.title: Luke 24:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ is authour, object, matter, and mark of Old and New Testament: the Babe of Bethlehem is bound up, (as I may so say) in these swathingbands: Turn we the eyes of our minds to him, as the Cherubins did their faces toward the Mercy-seat. The Angels do, 1 Pet. 1. 12.

entries.title: Luke 24:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So did the Angel to Lot, Gen. 19. 2. See the like, Josh. 8. 5, 6. 1 King. 3. 24. If Salomon might make as though he would do an act that was unlawfull, we may surely do the like in things indifferent. Yet this was never done (as is well observed) but 1 by those that had authority over others. 2 For some singular good to them, with whom they thus dealt.

entries.title: Luke 24:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Though they had been sharply rebuked by him, whom they know to be no other then a meer stranger to them.

For it is toward evening] Cry we, now if ever, ere it be too late; Vespera jam venit, nobiscum Christe maneto. Extingui [ilegible] nec patiare [ilegible].

entries.title: Luke 24:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Its thought they knew him by his ordinary form of giving thanks before meat.

entries.title: Luke 24:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
By that spirit of burning Esay 4. 4. that kindleth the fire of God, Cant. 8. 6. on the harth of his Peoples hearts, whiles the mystery of Christ is laid open unto them. Ego verò illius oratione sic incendebar, (saith Senarclaeus, (Senarc. in [ilegible] pist. ad Bucer.) concerning Diarius the Martyr) ut cùm eum disserentem audirem, Spiritus sancti verba me audire existimarem. Me thoughts when I heard him, I heard the Holy Ghost himself speaking to me.

While he opened] Preaching then is the key of the Scripture.

entries.title: Luke 24:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Late though it were, and they weary, yet they return the same night, not sparing themselves to do good to others.

entries.title: Luke 24:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: With those stamps of dishonour that the Jewes did me with wicked hands. These he retained even after his Resurrection, as for the confirmation of his Apostles, so for our instruction, not to think much to suffer losse of honour for our brethrens good and comfort.

entries.title: Luke 24:44
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: When a book is set forth, verses of commendation, are oft set afore it. Christ by this one sentence hath more honoured and authorized the book of [ilegible], then all men could have done by their Prefaces and Elogies prefixed thereunto. The Turks disclaime both Testaments, yet swear (D. Hakew in his Davids Vow.) as solemnly by the Psalms of David, as by the Alchoran of Mahomet.

entries.title: Luke 24:47
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Blessed be God (saith one) that after our ship-wrack by Adam, there is such a plank as Repentance for a poor sinner to swim to heaven upon. It is a mourning for sin, as it is offensivum Dei, & aversivum a Deo. It is commissa plangere, & plangenda non committere, as Ambrose hath it: to bewaile what is done amisse, and to do so no more.

entries.title: Luke 24:49
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Cloathed. Carnall men ([ilegible].) are naked men: when the Saints are arrayed with that fine [ilegible] linnen and shining, Rev. 19. 8.

entries.title: Luke 24:50
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Where his three dear friends dwelt, Lazarus, Martha, and Mary. From hence he went to his crosse, and from hence he would go to his crown.

He lift up his hands] As a good houshoulder, or rather as the high-Preist of the New Testament: benedixit, id est, valedixit, he blessed them, and so bade them Farewell.

entries.title: Luke 24:52
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yet could they not hear of his ascending to the Father, without great sorrow, John 14. and 16. We greive for that sometimes that we have great cause to take comfort in; such is our weaknesse and waywardnesse.

entries.title: Luke 24:53
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Inter laudum [ilegible], promissum Spiritus sancti adventum, promptis per omnia paratisque (Beda.) cordibus exspectant. So putting themselves into a fit posture to receive the Comforter that Christ had promised them.
